Making his first visit to the wonder

devoted the whole day to sightseeing.
There were no speeches, and politics

grandeur of rugged, snow-topped peaks
and wild. Rocky Mountain streams.


The presidential party left the

Standard time) at Gardiner, Mont,

Immediately through Theodore Roose-
velt Arch.


The temperature was below freezing

we're bundled in robes in the rear
seat of an open car. He wore a
tweed sport suit and light topcoat.
She wore fur coat and hiking shoes.
Senator Murray, Democrat, of Mon
tana was with them. Representative
OConnor, Democrat, of Montana rode
on the front seat.

The Senator and Representative and

Joined the party when the train

The Presidents first sight inside the

against a rugged mountain back
ground.


A snake-like motor trail along the
Gardiner and Boiling Rivers brought

its two-day park visit.


During brief pause here, Edmund

Smaller mountains along the route

Geese and swan glided across

At Artists Point, on the Yellowstone

MADRID, March II d.N.S0.
Fighting in SPANS civil war took
to the air today as all land fronts
save the Cordoba sector were re-
ported quiet.


But on virtually all fronts recon
naissance and fighting planes Of
both sides continued operations,
which have increased in intensity
during the past few days.


Heavy fighting was reported
around the Cordoba area, and
loyalist officials said many italian
troops were helping the insurgents
there.


The newspaper La Voz reported
1,407 persons killed and 3,488
wounded by insurgent bombing
raids and shelling of Madrid be-
tween october 23 and the end of
February. There were 10 air raids
on Madrid during November.


Official figures, said the paper,
show $50 buildings in the capital
were either totally or partially
affected" by bombs, including IA
schools, eight churches, four hos
pitals and nine homes for the aged.


Loyalist planes raided insurgent
positions at Brihuega. dropping
760 bombs. Thirty pursuit planes
then machine-gunned the same
positions.


Later, an aerial battle took
place over Guadalajara, the in.
surgents losing three machines
and the loyalists one.


AMSTERDAM, March II G.N.S).
The 1,464-ton Dutch cargo steamer,
Jonge Johanna, carrying a cargo
Of coal from Holland to France,
has been seized off Ceuta, Morocco,
by Spanish insurgent warship.


The Jonge Johanna sent out an
S o S when the warship ap-
preached, and the Dutch cruiser
Hertzog Hendrix, cruising in the
straits of Gibraltar, rushed full
speed to the rescue, but arrived too
late.


The insurgents took the Jonge
Johanna into Ceuta. The cruiser
refrained from following for fear
Of being sunk by the insurgents.


The incident was believed the
reason for yesterdays sudden prep
aration of four Dutch submarines
for dispatch to Spanish waters.

Amid the clamor for a special ses-

since 1929.


The Bureau Of Agricultural Eco
nomics estimated the farm cash in
come for the United States during
the first eight months of this year
at $685., 100000. This was nearly
s700,000,000 more than farmers re-
ceived in the January-August period
last year.


The income estimates we're based on
a survey Of principal farm products
marketed and Government payments
to farmers. The data extended only
through August and did not reflect
the sharp drop in cotton prices,
chief cause of the special session
plea.

cultural regions showed income gains
over last year, with the largest in
creases in the Southern States that
depend chiefly on cotton and tobacco.

experts today greeted an exhibition of
styles for Fall that was literally and
frankly a revelation of how scant

was very old-and on with the new
provided there was not too much of
it. "Scant raiment" was officially the
theme Of the Schiaparelli show and

daring decollete evening gown, sum-
med up the trend:


Primarily clothes have become an
index to the beauty and vitality of

Evening gowns were cut revealingly

other surprises in a show that had
for its keynote:


Away with all inhibitions."


There were hats named foolish
virgin" and suppressed desire" and

worn as shoes-kid evening sandals

pockets were not pockets but inviting

embroidery.

of silver fox had pink eyes ana a
cunning ribbon tied about it's neck
Other furs were dyed crimson red
and prickly pear green and there was
a trimmed glove in 10 colors-a
color for each finger.


Just for contrast there were styles
from the days when grandmother was
a girl styles that brought wistful
memories Of the Victorian era and the
mauve decade of the gay nineties with
notifications of the hoop skirt end
just suggestion OF hustle.


Sport coats featured trimming and
Innings Of dark-colored plaids or
stripes with berets of plaid to match.


The day silhouette was kept straight
and narrow for suits and dresses but
not as straight as one evening creation
which fitted straight over the body
like q tube.


Afternoon coats had fitted waists

or heavy embroideries Of gold, Gold
and jeweled embroidery was also fea-
tured for velvet cocktail and dinner
jackets worn with crepe or broadcloth
dresses.

bright red wool trousers to be worn

three Judge hearing.

Testimony that the hostess in the
Willard Hotel Coffee Shop, Miss Evelyn
Miller, called Mrs. Mabel Norman the
best waitress" in the shop and then
notified her Of her discharge on the
grounds of incompetence" was placed
before the National Labor Relations
Board yesterday in hearings on the
boards complaint that Mrs Norman
was dismissed because of testimony
against the hotel management in a
previous case before the board.


The testimony of yesterday was that
of Miss Maude Card, who told Trial
Examiner Edwin S. Smith that Miss
Miller told her on the night of Mrs.
Normans discharge that the latter was
the best waitress" in the shop and
that she could always depend" on
her. A few minutes later Miss Card
said she heard Miss Miller tell Mrs
Norman that her dismissal was because
Of Incompetence.


How could you say that after
what you just told me?" Miss Card
said she asked Miss Miller. "Oh, you
know why she's fired" she then quoted
Miss Miller as saying.


Miss Doris Middleton, another
waitress at the shop. said she re-
fused to sign petition asking the
Hotel and Restaurant Workers Alli-
ance, of which Mrs. Norman was a
member. to transfer Mrs. Norman to
another hotel. She admitted however,
that she thought friction among the
girls might have been decreased by
Mrs. Norman's transfer.


Miss Angela Harrison, another
waitress, told the board that Mrs.
Norman was ''cocky' toward the su-
pervisers and other mattresses. Miss
Lottie Newman, another waitress, Of
fered similar testimony and said that
this attitude has been accentuated
since Mrs. Norman joined the union
last December.


AS yesterdays hearing opened,
Smith cautioned the witnesses sharply
against being evasive and instructed
them to answer all questions fully
and frankly. He denied request by
counsel for the hotel to have the
hearings in executive session.


The hearings will continue tomor-
row afternoon with the respondent
planning to bring on approximately a
dozen more witnesses.

BY MORRIS ]. HARRIS,

SHANGHAI. Oct. 27-Historic
Chapel, world-renowned since the clash
of Chinas 18th Route Army with the
Japanese in 1882, met its final doom
tonight.


Whipped by southerly wind. miles
of flame swept through what was left
of this one-time humanity packed city
which again became battlefield Au-
gust 13 The fires started early today,
when the Chinese resistance to the
japanese collapsed.


The scenes here tonight were vir-
tually identical to those I saw in 1882,
when the terrific struggle ended. as it
did today, with a sudden Chinese with
drawal before the relentless punish
ment of the japanese mechanical army
and navy.


Fire RACES Uncontrolled.


Stretching from we'll toward Kiang-
wan southwark into Chapel to the
very edges of the International Settle
ment, thence westward for an unde-
termined number of miles, uncon-
trolled fire swept whatever was in It's
path.


Patches of shell-torn but thus far
unburned buildings dotted this huge
area in which courageous Chinese
troops, refusing to retreat before the
japanese thrust, fought on.


But they seemingly were destined
to be engulfed in the flames if jap
anese bullets did not bring a speedier
end


Vast sheets of flame shot toward the
sky. The heat was so intense it was
felt throughout the city.


Firemen from the International Set
tlement, deployed on the south bank
of Soochow Greek, continued to fight
to save the foreign area from de-
struction. In single area where the
flames jumped the creek $50 build
ings were burned, but the firemen
said the fire was under control


Flames Light Horizon.


Beyond the western borders of the
Settlement, where the Chinese and
japanese seemingly were preparing to
resume their fighting, additional fires
lighted the horizon. All Shanghai to
the south of the creek watched this
awesome sight, braving the dangers
of stray bullets and shell fragments
which continued to come.


1t was a repetition of 1882 on a
erander scale. Being a survivor of
Japan's great earthquake September
/, 1928, 1 saw Toxic and Yokohama
burn in fires resulting from that dis
aster. Tonight recalled those horrors


Chapel will be blackened ruins
devoid of life before the flames,
threatening all Shanghai, subside.


Flames penetrated the Settlement at
one point and by midafternoon had
consumed square block of closely
packed houses on Tibet road.


Both Sides Start Fires.


The fires were started by both Chi
nese and japanese. Chinese put
torches to buildings to cover their
retreat from positions they had held
for more than two months. Japanese
did likewise to drive Chinese rear
guard snipers from barricades and
blasted ruins.


British and American defense forces
guarding settlement borders against
possible military emergencies became
fire guards as well.


AS the flames roared ON, japanese
warplanes strafed retreating Chinese
with bombs and machine gun bullets.
The japanese announced their forces
had occupied Chapel, but said num-
ber of isolated Chinese units re-
manned.


Foes Face. Across Soochow Greek.


Just west of the Settlement boundary
Chinese and japanese Armies faced
each other from opposite banks of
winding, muddy Soochow Greek.
Generalissimo Chang Kai-shek's war
riors dug in along the southern bank
of the creek, prepared to force jap
anese to wage another major engage
ment.


British defenders closed barbed
wire gates and refused to permit any
more refugees fleeing from Japanese
to enter the Settlement. Thousands
of Chinese surged against the barri-
cades, screaming in terror, but Brit
ish declared opening the gateway
would imperil the Settlement.


Because machine gun fire endan-
gered the Settlements western border,
the British consul general warned all
British nationals to be ready to
evacuate dangerous territory. Ameri-
can officials were considering possible
similar action.

at railroad bridge across Soochow
Greek, just outside st. Johns Uni
versity campus, fell back to a safer
post near Jessfield Park. The troops

CHICAGO, May 22.-Uncle Sam re-
turned tt. the butter market this week

desire to stabilize" prices.


After an absence of almost year.

by private traders, showed its

traders had been bandying about
the trade unconfirmed gossip that
"the angel was watching the
market but the Government agents
kept good poker faces

Seven-year-old Hazel Machican, one

farm home since Sunday when they
set out to look for strayed cattle, was

terday.


She was found in the dense bush
country 20 miles northwest of the

seen.

hundreds of volunteers pressed their
search for her 9-year-old companion,
Lena Shkraba, who, Hazel said, had

set by the younger child.


Lena and Hazel disappeared Sun
day and have been hunted night and
day. Fears were expressed the chill
dren had been attacked by bears.

found yesterday in slough several
miles from home He had wandered
away Saturday and was suffering
from exposure when rescued.


He was rushed to a hospital in
Humboldt, where it was believed he
would recover.

appendix, closed the wound.

NEW YORK, February 27-With
rampant metals holding the bit in
their teeth, commodity prices swept to
the highest level since early 1880 in
the latest week.


Price movements again emphasized
the opposite courses being traced by
the two principal staple groups
products of the farm and industrial
raw materials. The former have been
drifting lower for the past fortnight;
the latter, paced by metals, have
jumped to new peaks for the recovery
swing.


The Associated Press weighted index
of 35 important wholesale commodities
inched ahead to 90.83 per cent of the
1926 average from 9049 a week ago,
and compared with 1888 in the same
period last year.


In the short span of two months,
the non-ferrous metal index has
rocketed 20 per cent. Last week
prices maintained the same trend;
antimony, tin, lead and copper rising
under heavy demand.


Some Hesitation Seen.


Some hesitation was noticed in the
headlong boom, however, as commod-
ity men pointed out substantially in
creased shipments could be expected
from mines in a few months. Mean
time the shortage in certain items
acted to buoy quotations.


Climbing steel scrap prices have re-
suited from the fast tempo of mill
operations and limitations to the
amount of pig iron companies can get
for fabricating steel. A shortage of
coke is partly responsible, as is a
dearth of furnaces.


Other industrial staples--rubber,
bituminous coal and lumber-con-
CURED in the advance.


Farm products. on the other hand,
yielded to the pressure of larger sup
plies and a hesitant demand. Agri-
cultural staples led the decline; corn,
wheat, oats and rye losing substantial
ly. Cotton alone breasted the tide,
responding to bullish reports regarding
mill activity.


Foods Fall Back.


Foods fell back. Eggs weakened as
supply continued large, despite Gov
eminent buying for relief distribution.
Sugar, coffee and flour were also
lower, while cocoa and lard managed
to exc out small gains.


Live stock and textiles were mixed.
Cattle and wool improved, lambs and
silk slipped.

MIAMI, Fla, January 16-Con-
tinuing with its parade Of events Of
national interest, Florida tomorrow
offers its Winter visitors from the
North an attractive diversion with
the opening Of the annual metropoli-
tan deep sea fishing tournament.


While approximately $4,000 North
ern sportsmen, and women, too. COM
peted last season for $4,000 in
trophies, the event has been made
more enticing this season, with the
total prize valuation having been
boosted to $4,000.


A hotilla Of fishing craft, valued
at many hundreds Of thousands Of
dollars, will file out, inaugurating the
opening Of the tournament, which
will end April IS. The marine parade
will start in Biscayne Bay and con-
tinue through Government Cut, where
the boats will spread in fan formation
and then head for the Gulf Stream
to take part in the days sport.


Sponsor of the tournament. the
Miami Rod and Reel Club, which has
an exclusive membership of 400
sportsmen from coast to coast and
from New Zealand, Canada and Cuba,
will be the center Of activity through
the months of competition.


Twenty-Seven varieties Of game fish
have been declared eligible for entry
in the tournament. They are blue
marlin, white marlin, sailfish, tarpon.
wahoo, tuna. African pompano, allison
tuna, amberjack. barracuda, bonefish,
bonito, dolphin, cobia, grouper, jack,
kingfish, mako shark, permit, redfish,
pompano trout. blue-fin tuna, snap
per, snook, ladyflsh and mackerel.


Weigh-in stations have been estab-
lished at Miami, Miami Beach, Bimini
and Key Largo.


Main requirement is that fish must
be caught within established boun-
daries and hooked with rod and reel
and without any assistance given the
angler.

LONDON, January 16.-The anoint-
ing of King George VI. the most i'm
portant part of the coronation cere-
mony, will be carried out with pure
olive oil. which will previously have
been consecrated by the Archbishop of
Canterbury, who will place the Oil
during the ceremony on the Kings
head, breast and palms. AS soon as
the ceremony has been completed, the
King will become the Lords
anointed"


The ceremony is the most impress
sive and solemn part of the corona
ton ritual. The King will remove
his crimson robes and will take his
seat in the great Kings chair, while
four Knights of the Garter hold a
golden pail over him. A spoon con-
tanning the consecrated oil, poured
from the golden Ampulla, will be
handed to the Archbishop, who will
carry out the ritual.


The spoon is the Oldest article in
the regalia, and has been in use since
the fifteenth century.

Inside Sibley Hospitals brick
walls all was warm and serene, in
sharp contrast to the chilling
rains outside, which sent the stray
pedestrian scurrying for shelter.


Patients had been tucked in
for the night. Save for the dim
light on the senior nurses desk,
the wards were dark.


White-clad interneS, moving
silently in their rubber-soled shoes,
we're making their rounds.


But in the nurses quarters
there was an air of hushed ex-
pectancy that even the natural
decorum of the hospital failed to
subdue. The Gaping service"
was about to start.


NOVICES IN LTNTELIGHT


In the hospital chapel, with
it's softly playing organ, dimmed
lights and stained glass windows,
nurses filled the black walnut
pews. Here were the post-gradu.
ates, in starched white, the black
velvet bands on their caps de-
noting their rank. Here, too,
we're the senior nurses all in
white and the juniors in blue
uniforms with white aprons and
caps. All fairly breathed cleanli-
ness and health.


Cynosure Of all eyes were two
rows Of young girls whose barred
heads denoted their probationship.
Their fresh young faces fairly
shone but their eyes were grave
and each held an united candle
in her meekly-folded hands.


THEIR ACID TEST


For the majority it was the most
important moment of their lives.
Tonight meant the end of their six
months probationship. No longer
would they be condescendingly re-
ferred to as "the probes; nor
given the most menial tasks, or be
politely snubbed, to teach them
the proper humility.


It meant, too, that they had
qualified: that they possessed the
characteristics so essential to the
good trained nurse-devotion to
duty, patience, tolerance, under.
standing and the ability to sacri.
flee themselves for the lame, the
sick, the halt and the blind.


CAP SACRED SYMBOL


The organ had stopped playing.
Now the superintendent of nurses
was speaking. The cap, she said.
was bestowed as q sacred trust,
which they must never betray.
She talked thus for 10 minutes.
Then the first probationer's name
was called.


Only the rustling of her starched
apron was heard as she rose.
walked to the altar and knelt. In
the hush that followed the superin.
tendent selected a cap from the
row before her and placed It on
the girls bowed head. Another
nurse helped pin 1t in place.


MURMUR PRAYER


The girl murmured a brief
prayer, rose and turned to meet
junior nurse, carrying a lighted
candle. Saying softly:


with the affection Of an
older sister I pass onto you the
light Of this school," she lighted
the others candle. It's yellow
glow Illuminated their young


Then the next girls name was
called-and the next and the next
Until all had received their caps.
With the candlelight on their faces
they made an unforgettable pic
ture - more like angels than
nurses


Followed a brief prayer, deem
notes OF the organ, and all was
over.

Frederick D. Grab, of Chicago,

of South America two weeks ago,
was found dead when a searching
party finally located the wreckage.
the State Department announced
today. Grabs death was disclosed

son, American Minister to Vene-
Zuela.


Another American passenger on
the Inflated ship, William Arm
strong Perry, New York newspaper
correspondent, escaped without
serious injury, Nicholson reported.


The plane plunged into the jun
giles during a violent storm two
weeks ago. So thick was the UNI
dergrowth that planes sent out in
search of the missing ship were
unable to locate it. Two native
members of the crew, the co-pilot
and radio man, who escaped Seri-
Gus injury, managed to fight their
way overland to q native village
with the news.


After a Today foot search the
ship was located and q messenger
sent back to Eldorado. Grab lived
for several days after the crash.

legation last night.

XI told Adolf Hitler today that the
Catholic Church must be left free to
fulfill its mission in Nazi Germany.


The pontiff's reply to the recent
German church note, which itself was
reply to the Pope's pre- Easter en-
cyclical accusing the German govern
ment OF violating the 1888 church.
state concordat, was delivered by
Eugenio Cardinal Pacelli to the Ger
man Ambassador to the Holy See, Diego
Won Bergen


Vatican sources said the note did
not mention Hitler's May day speech,
when he warned against sermons or
"encyclicals' which disturb" the
Third Reich. It took more moderate
tone than the encyclical, and left the
way open for further conversations
about the concordat, which set up
separate spheres of church and state
influence in the Reich.


The note maintained, however. the
church's insistence that economic
pressure must not be brought to bear
against Catholics in Germany; that
Catholic schools and the Catholic
press should not be hampered.

The Senate today was asked

Byrd reorganization committee

President Roosevelt's program for
reorganizing the Federal Govern

Two resolutions, sponsored by
the Administration, would accom-

Senate consent to creation Of
Joint congressional committee for
handling the program, with the
Senate represented by nine Sen.
ators. The Senate group would
include six Democrats, two Repub-
licans and one Independent.


The second resolution would
make these nine Senators a per-
manent Senate committee for han
ding reorganization legislation.
Previously, such legislation would
have gone to the special commit
tee that worked all summer under
Senator Harry Flood Byrd CD OF
Virginia on reorganization plans.


Byrd probably will be made a
member Of the new committee and
serve on the joint committee. Ad-
ministration leaders regard him as
unfriendly to the Presidents re-
organization plan, since he has
demanded reorganization for the
purpose of reducing the cost Of
Government, as well as to increase
efficiency. The Presidents plan
would include no economies and
might even increase Government
costs.

ship on the proposed new com.
mittee would give the AdminiStra-
tion complete control Of recon-
mendations. On the Byrd COM
mittee, which included but three
Democrats and two Republicans,
Byrd had control by uniting with
the Republicans. This was The
Administrations reason for elimi-

Spanish Flag at Stern

to be frightened and continued

the British destroyers arrived.

version, the Canarias made off"

sensational race against time and
the United States Congress, sailed
from New York with its cargo

February %, its hold loaded with

The Federal Trade Commission filed

oppression and coercion to compel
dealers handling General Motors cars,

accessories and supplies for use on

chises to sell General Motors cars If

ST. JEAN DE LUZ, France,
Sept. 20 GN.S). - Fighting
against poorly-organized Asturian
troops in the mountains of north
ern Spain, insurgent columns to-
day labored slowly towards Gijon,
but Spanish government militia
men reported progress on the Sara
gossa front.


On the sea, the insurgent cruiser
Canarias routed three loyalist de-
stroyers in an hours battle and
captured two cargo ships, one Of
them the Rey Jaime.


BOMBS MISS SHIP


In retaliation, loyal airplanes
pursued the Canarias off the Cata-
lonian coast, but their bombs
missed her.


Fierce, but indecisive fighting
went on along the eastern front,
where the insurgent pounded loyal
positions with artillery and aerial
bombs around Zuera.


The insurgents then followed up
with an attack by grenade-throw-
ing infantrymen, but they were
driven off by well-placed machine
guns with heavy losses.


CARRYING WAR CARGOES


In the south, the loyalists gained
Mulva Peak, but lost it in VIC
lent insurgent counter-attack.


Announcing that the insurgent
advance continues on the Asturias
and Leon fronts, a communique
issued at Salamanca said that 10
new hill posts we're established,
and Mt. Lacalva in Leon was
taken.


When captured by the Canarias,
it was said, the two merchant
ships were bound for loyalist ports
with cargoes of war materials,
trucks, and supplies. Both ships
were escorted to Palma, Majorca

text:
FOLSOM PRISON, Cal, Sept.
20 GN.S)-Folsom's band Of riot
ing convicts, who staggered with
murderous cruelty yesterday,
cringed in the prison hospital to-
day under heavy guard and Writ
ually begged for death from their
wounds rather than face Califor-
MAS new method of execution
the lethal gas chamber.


The bloody escape plot in which
Guard H. E. Martin and two con-
victs were slain and eight others,
including five of the rioters,
Warden Clarence Larkin, Captain
Of the Guard william Ryan and
Guard James Kearns we're seriously
wounded, already was the subject
Of a sweeping probe by the State
Prison Board of Directors.


LOCKED IN CELLS


While the probe was underway
Folsom's $500 convicts-hardened
two time losers"-were kept in
their cell blocks,


Occasional jeers and catcalls
echoed through the prison, indicat-
ing the seething unrest caused by
yesterdays futile break for free
dom which was the most violent
uprising in this powder key"
since the bloody Thanksgiving Day
riot in 1927 when nine convicts
and two guards were killed and "a
wounded.


District Attorney Otis D. Bah
cock declared that he would per
sonalIy prosecute the five convict
survivors.


The prison board was anxious
to determine how the plotters were
able to fashion 10 knives from
files and other tools and to make
two wooden pistols, and where
they found a 20-pound piece of
steel which was welded with
terrific force after the criminals
had gained entrance to the cap
tain Of the guards office shortly
before noon yesterday.


Guard May Die


Meanwhile, in the prison hos
pital Warden Larkin, stabbed IL
times; Guard Captain Ryan. stab
bed seven times, and Guard
Kearns, also stabbed, were re-
ported "holding their own" Their
condition was described as serious.
Kearns may die.


In another section of the prison
hospital were Ed Davis, Los
Angeles "lifer," and leader of the
break; Robert Lee Cannon.
burglar: Fred Barnes, Los Angeles
robber; Albert Kessell, San Fran
cisco robber, and Wesley E. Eudy,
Pomona robber and parole
violator.


Davis and Cannon were re-
ported near death.


CONVICTS SLAIN


The two convicts slain were
CLYDE Stevens, notorious San
Francisco bank robber, who pro-
vded the guns for the San QUEEN
tin prison kidnapping and prison
break Of January, 1885; and Ben
ME Kucharski, Los Angeles robber,
serving life sentence.


The escape plot was foolhardy
and desperate for, even if the
rioters had managed to get past
the inner prison gate, they would
have met death before passing
the three outer gates and guard
towers which surround the prison

BY the Associated Press.


BUENOS AIRES, August l7-Revo-
lutionary communicates from Asuncion
and statements by Paraguayans in
exile here today attributed the down.
fall of Paraguay's provisional President,
Col. Rafael Franco, to a displeased
army.


Most OF the causes were linked with
the now stalemated Chaco War be-
tween the Impoverished inland re-
public and Bolivia.


An army-navy coup last Friday
forced resignation OF the Franco cabi-
net. Yesterday the reorganization was
completed by appointment of Dr.
Felix Paiva, dean of the University
Law School, to succeed Franco.


Army Dissa tisfied.


Among the causes for the govern
mental switch were the army'S dis
satisfaction over neutral military regu-
lations governing the military status
Of the Western Chaco, its displeasure
over Frances treatment Of Gen. Jose
Felix Estigarribia and its belief that
Franco was not pushing projected agri-
cultural and social reforms.


Franco really began to slip last jan
uary when the Uruguay conference OF
neutralS issued regulations for super
vision OF the zone separating military
lines in the Western Chaco Paraguay
was requested to withdraw troops for
several miles in one section hit when
Franco tried to comply, the men re-
fused stating they would not give up
any ground won during the long Chaco
War.


Dispute Has Lasted Since Then.


Franco and some Paraguayan mill
tary leaders have been In dispute since
that time.


Several weeks ago Franco tried to
send other attachments to the Chaco
from Asuncion to impose his will, but
the officers refused to carry out his
orders. Finally the present Chaco
commander, Lieut. Col Ramon Para
des, who is also chief Of the army,
sent Franco what amounted to an
ultimatum.


This resulted in the resignation Of
his cabinet, then Frances own with
drawal.


Inasmuch as the Chaco conference
has been trying for 4 year without
success to discuss settlement, the
status quo was considered likely to
last possibly for years.

By the Associated Press


HENDAYE, Franco-Spanish From
tier, August l7.-Generalissimo Fran
cisco Frances legions lunged against
the tottering defenses OF Santander
from five directions today. Insurgent
tacticians predicted the fall OF the
Biscayan capital within a week.


One powerful column, which ripped
open path with hand grenades and
bayonets, was reported to have routed
Spanish government troops from
Escudo Pass, Santander's last noun
tain stronghold on the south, and to
be within 80 miles Of It's coastal
objective.


A dispatch from the insurgent side
said seven government battalions had
been trapped by Frances fast moving
offensive and that the number of
government dead had reached the
thousands. The insurgent command
claimed the governments northern
defense had been demoralized.


Reinosa Taken Yesterday.


The important manufacturing CEN
ter OF Reinosa, about 80 miles south
and slightly west of Santander in the
heart of rich mineral lands, was cap
tured by one tnsurgent column yes
terday.


A government report, while not
mentioning Reinosa specifically, said
g. Slight retreat" had been carried
out because Of "the important num-
Der of war elements which the enemy
brought into use"


These elements" included one of
the heaviest aerial attacks Of the
13-months civil war.


Government machine gunners and
rif1emen tried to hold ReinoSa with
q house toulouse defense, but finally
were overpowered and put to flight
by the superior strength of the attack
ing force.


The insurgent communicate said
the occupation of Reinosa gave Franco
control of large factory known as
the CONSTRUCTOR naval" manufactur-
ing marine engines, naval equipment
and munitions.


30 Miles From Santa nder.


The swift thrust of another column
along the Palencia -Burgos road
brought the insurgent advance guard
within 30 miles OF Santander. More
than 20 villages we're captured by the
insurgents yesterday.


Foreign legionnaires under Frances
banners were described as largely re-
sponsible for the complete defeat
Of the enemy"


Residents Of occupied villages gave
Joyous welcomes to the conquertng
insurgents, Frances communique said


The civil population of Reinosa
normally $4,000, had been reduced
sharply by evacuation recently.


Besides two columns driving north
ward toward Santander, three other
segments of Frances army were on
the move along the coast. east OF the
seaport, and in the rolling country
to it's southeast.

THE method by which grapefruit are
- harvested determines the extent to
which rotting Of the fruit develops and
the practices of 80 and 40 years ago
are found far superior to modern
methods Of harvesting the fruit. ac-
cording to the Department Of Agri-
culture


When the fruit is pulled from the
tree rather than clipped of, the dan
ger Of rot is greatly decreased.


The reason Is logical enough. The
fungus which causes rotting develops
In dead twig ends and soon spreads
to the fruit. However, when the fruit
is pulled from the tree, the dead ends
are eliminated, the twig being COM
pletely taken from the tree and from
the fruit.


As remedy for rot, the fruit is
dropped into a weak borax solution
after being harvested, but clipped fruit
20 treated develops rot faster than
pulled fruit which Is not treated.


Thirty days after harvesting, clipped
and untreated fruit show 40 per cent
rotting. Treated clipped fruit show
about Is per cent. Untreated pulled
fruit shows about 13 per cent and
pulled treated fruit about II per cent
AL this indicates that in some cases
at least, the old methods are best.

NEW YORK, Jan. 13 UN.sJ.
Less than SO hours after the bath
tub Staying Of Mrs. Mary Harriet
Case, 25, in her jackson Heights
apartment. police announced they
had found the killer in the person
of a colored porter who worked in
the building.


The colored man was identified
as Major Green, 80, formerly en-
ployed by the Jackson Heights
Bachelors Club. Police said three
of his fingerprints were found on
the door of the bathroom where
the flimsily-clad body of Mrs.
Case. beaten and strangled, had
been thrown.


Arrested with Green and grilled
as accessories after the fact were
his brother, Henry Green. and Will
liam Henry johnson, nephew of
Green's wife. johnson. police said.
sent to laundry a bloodstained
shirt belonging to Major Green,
and Henry Green tried to dispose
Of suit Of clothes alleged to have
been taken from the Case apart
ment.


Authorities believe Green, find
ing the Apartment door unlocked,
entered with the intention of rob
bing the Case home. Mrs. Cases
wedding ring and her husbands
suit were missing when Case
found his wife dead in the bath
tub.


Despite what police described
as "damning evidence" Green
stolidly denied his guilt, resisting
an all-night grilling. When police
took him to the blood-spattered
Case home shortly before dawn
and re-enacted the crime, showing
him where the petite woman had
been struck down, dragged across
the floor, strangled and thrust in
an overflowing bathtub. the man
remained unmoved.

diplomatic dress, passed down the re-
ceiving line. His three daughters ac-
companied him.


The two ENJOYS and their staffs
slipped punch in the state dining room
at the same time, but stood in sepa-
rate groups. Ambassador Saito and
his aides remained only half an hour,
and shortly after their departure the
Chinese Ambassador left.


The reception, traditionally the most
colorful of the year, honored repre-
sentatives Of 81 countries.

Standard Oil Co., was entering the
Hainan Straits in the South China

Thousands of early season vacA-

New York and Montreal are finding
Au Sable Chasm offers scenic won-
amaze the casual visitor. Even great
scientists are unable to say Just what
caused this gigantic fault in the sand
stone structure Of the earth's surface
through which the Au Sable River
roars and tumbles on its way from
the Adirondacks to the peaceful
reaches Of Lake Champlain.


Situated in historic territory, ~
miles south of Plattsburg and only
a few miles from Lake Champiain,
ports of call is the great chasm Of the
Au Sable River, famous for over 4
century for its weird beauty and
strange geologic formations.


The chasm is accessible throughout
the entire mile and half OF its
length. In places sheer sandstone
cliffs tower over 100 feet into the
blue, the walls rising layer on layer.
frequently in such precise alignment
that they might have been 30 placed
by some master mason in prehistoric
days.


Winding walks in places follow the
waters edge and again they cross the
great chasm with the wild waters far
below. From table rock, a little
more than half way through this nat
ural wonder, sturdy boats, manned by
trained north country boatmen, take
the explorer down through the
"f1ume" and the swirling rapids and
out into the open country.

could not be made until Japan had

ment it was not essential that China

The vice minister for foreign affairs
Kensuke Horinouchi, told the British
charge a'affaires, J. l.. Dodds, the
Japanese government believes only
japanese troops can protect japanese
lives and property so long as the
Chinese troops remain. Britain sug-
gested Japan and China withdraw

terests to the joint protection of

Amplifying the Japanese position

Chinese troops must withdraw far
enough beyond the limits of the 1882
demilitarized zone to make a posi-

say whether Japanese troops woulG

Pile, that Japan did not desire to

ciple Of japanese policy that Chinese
activity against Japan and Manchu-
kuo, its protege state, must be stopped

With the beginning Of the new
year, the World Calendar Associa-
ton reports rapid strides throughout
the world during the last IL months
in the direction of calendar reform.


Foremost among developments
pointed to were Endorsements of the
movement by the American States
Labor Conference. held at Santiago,
Chile. and the International Labor
Conference, held at Geneva, Switzer-
lano. last June


Only a few weeks ago, the aSsocia.
tion stated, the Central Statistical
Board, Government co-ordinating
group, made public a report to the
Secretary of State urging revision Of
the calendar.


From England and her dominions,
France. Germany. Switzerland, Bel
gium. Greece, Japan and China, as
we'll as the Latin American countries,
comes support for the reform.


The reform plan would divide the
year into four equal parts, each quar-
ter having three months. of which the
first month would have 81 days and
the other two 80 days each. In order
TO make the calendar perpetual, the
365th day would would fall each year
after December 80. and in leap years
the 366th day would be placed in mid.
Summer, after June 80.

By the Associated Press.


HONG KONG, September Fire
caused by disastrous typhoon, ragged
through Hong Kong today after a 1875
mile-an-hour wind had taken hun
dreds of lives ashore and at sea. The
death toll, steadily rising, was believed
to have passed 500. Officials expressed
fear it would mount into thousands.


A wide area of this British Crown
colony was devastated and waist-deep
in water. Large and small ships were
piled up on the sea wall and strewn
in the submerged water front streets.


Distress calls from laundering ships
poured in from all sides. Shipping
suffered particularly heavily in the
gale, one of the worst in Hong Kongs
history, because the harbor Is
thronged with refugee-laden ships
from the Shanghai war zone and
steamers that have taken haven from
the japanese coastal blockade.


One of the foundered steamers was
the liner Human, carrying 1900 Chi
nese refugees from the Shanghai
sector.


Dutch Liner Is Lost.


The 4,552-ton Dutch liner Van
Heutsz was total loss. Two Of the
largest ships in the harbor, the 18,765-
ton Lloyd Trietino liner Conte Verde
and the 16,975-ton Japanese liner
Asama Maru, were swept ashore.


Two British ships, the Mausang and
Boong Court, and the Chinese Queton
were reported sunk. The British
steamers Lyeemoon, Kalgan and
Kwangchow, the Norwegian freighter
Produce and the Chinese Shenglee
were pounded ashore


British police and revenue officers,
heroically forming human lifeline
strung together with ropes, rescued
the crews of many smaller stranded
ships and hundreds Of Chinese ref
ueees


Downtown Area Demolished.


The downtown area Of Hong Kong
was demolished as completely as If
it had been bombed. Streets were lit
tered with the debris Of shattered
windows, collapsed walls, blown-down
signs and the wrecks of automobiles.


Fifteen bodies were recovered from
the fire caused by the gale. It was
not known how many others were
trapped in the flames and ruins Of
caved-in buildings.


Countless scores of small craft were
tossed like chips against the seawall
and those who made them their
homes were drowned. Observatory
instruments ceased to function after
registering 125 mile an hour
velocity.


Fifty Chinese were reported to have
been killed almost instantly when a
block of buildings collapsed at Tai Pc.
Along the coast at Macao serious
damage was done, particularly to the
picturesque colony Of boat dwellers.

LONDON, September 2.-Britain,
reused to indignant action by the
mysterious sinking of a tanker and
the close escape of a destroyer from
unidentified submarines Off the Span
ish coast, ordered her fleet reinforced
today in the Western Mediterranean.


Informed circles said the govern
ment suspected Italy of responsibility
for strange and repeated assaults on
shipping of many nations off the
Spanish government coast, on the
narrow British empire "life line"


The tanker Woodford, flying the
British flag, went down off the east
coast of Spain, torpedoed yesterday
by an undersea craft near where
zigzagging by the British destroyer
Havock helped the warship dodge a
torpedo Tuesday night.


The Woodford's second engineer was
killed and six of her crew were in
tured.


Approved by French.


Authoritative sources said the cab
1net'S decision to rush more war
ships into the Mediterranean carried
full French approval. France has
warned that she will not tolerate mo-
lestation of shipping in waters vital
to her trade and colonial communi-
cations.


The order for reinforcements was
announced after tense cabinet men,
bers had attempted at two long ses-
sions to shape the empires policy
against the attacks on her ships


The Spanish government ambassa-
dor was summoned to the foreign Of
fee shortly before the second cabinet
meeting adjourned early this after
noon.


The possibility arose that the mys-
terious submarine that attacked the
Havock had been destroyed by the
Havock's defensive depth charges.


Members of the Havock's crew at
Gibraltar said the destroyer, sighting
the approaching torpedo, had zig
Jagged and dropped five depth bombs.


Then the Havock signaled to other
British warships and watch was kept
over a 15-mile radius. Soon oil ap-
peared on the surface, indicating, the
seamen believed, that the submarine
had been sunk.


Crew Takes to Boats.


The attack on the Woodford oc-
Cured about 70 miles north of where
the destroyer Havock was attacked.
The captain reported the ship sank
three hours after she was torpedoed
and that the crew took to the boats.
arriving at the town Of Benicarlo on
the west Spanish coast after eight
hours at sea.


The Earl of Perth, British Am
bassador to Rome, held surprise
interview with Eden before the min
listers met.


The whole Mediterranean question
is due for an airing at Geneva meet
ing of the League of Nations Septem-
Der 10, where Italy has been accused
by the Valencia regime of aggression
against Spanish government shipping.


The feeling here was that unless
italy disproved the Spanish charges
the future of Anglo-Italian friendship
talks would be virtually hopeless.

BENDIX, N. j., Dec. 13.--Three
persons owed their lives today to a
cool-headed professional stunt flyer
who landed his airplane safely after
a collision with another plane which
cost the life of John j. Diskon, 27-
year-old Paterson attorney.


About 400 feet above Bendix Air
port the right wing Of Diskon's plane
struck the landing gear Of the sight
seeing passenger plane yesterday. Its
wing sheared off, Diskon's plane
crashed, killing him instantly.


Pilot William Picune, 23 of North
Bergen. kept his plane in control and
when airport attendants signaled him
the undercarriage was not disabled, he
brought the ship safely to the ground
without injury to his three passen-
gers. He received slight injuries in
the collision.


Diskon had student pilot license.
Picune has been flying four years.

Britain, whose proposal that she and

keep the Spanish civil war confined
to Spain.

don, Charles Corbin, was understood

would end the system Of international
frontier supervision between France
and Spain the first Of next week un-
less the gaps In the sea patrol were
restored or British observers were re-
turned to their functions on the Port
uguese frontier


Britain and France acted to restore

Germany and Italy withdrew their
warships because of Spanish govern
ment attacks on them.

Meteors are strange things. No
one knows just how they are formed.
All one can say is that they are par
ticles of cosmic dust and that the
showers are disintegrated comets.
Many millions of them come into the
atmosphere every day but only few
hit the earth; the rest are consumed
by air friction. Admiral Byrd estimated
fifty millions day in the Antarctic.


When they strike the earth they
are cold. for they have been in space at
almost absolute zero. One fell in a
haystack without igniting the hay.
They may come into the atmosphere
at as high speed as fifty miles a
second; then friction heats up the
surface and produces streak of light.

Jannas room was in front of the inn where she
could sit on her wooden balcony and enjoy
the social activity of the street. Her friends
would pass and give her greeting and tell her
the doings of the day.


What could trouble us?" laughed Tasl
who are so used to trouble" Then catching
sight Of Yom and his father waiting for their
supper, she added: 81 must be gone about my
work Soon will come back to you


When she had gone, Janna turned the wheels
of her chair and drew back into the shadows
that she might watch, undisturbed and unseen.


1t had been market day in the neighboring
town, and the wide street was thronged with
people returning with their purchases. string
of silky white goats picked their way delicately
over the ruts and stones. The orange street
lamps shone on their crooked posts made of the
trunks of young trees. Across the street. the
sausage fryer piled his savory trade outside his
doorway. The women stood in groups and
gossiped. Three gypsies came along and began
to play their violins = Wild melancholy til
game melodies that tugged at the heart.


Janna saw Yom's dark face in the light from
the windows of the inn. He was Indifferent to
the exctements of the street Outside the village

-ASL halted the tired oxen under the shade


of vast tree. Then she lifted the old


woman out of the cart and propped her


against the wide comfortable trunk. She
put the water cooler in the sun and laid out the
provisions : dark peasant bread. square OF
goats cheese, basket of Strawberries.


The frail old woman heaved gusty sigh of
content. The ground felt good to her tired bones
and the shade was deep and cool. She watched
Tasl lovingly as the girl filled pail at the irr
cation runnel to water the oxen. The child was
grace itself, she thought Grace and strength
apd youth. At last Tasl threw herself on the
ground.


Grandmother, how hot it isl" she exclaimed.
She took off her black hood before she began
to eat


Outside the pool of darkness, cast by the roof
of the tree, the blazing MONDAY lay all about
them. Out of its brassy glare two horsemen
rode towards the promise of shade and rest. A
cloud of butterflies followed them like floating
flowers = crawling over their hands and set
Ting on the harness.


As they drew near the watchers saw that they
we're an elderly man and a very young man,
both handsome, black-eyed and debonair. the
younger almost a boy.


''How funny they look covered with the but
terflies." giggled Tasl When Yomi reined in his
little white Hungarian horse and brushed the
insistent insects from his person, she looked up
and laughed aloud at him.


Both men dismounted, and the elder in
quired courteously if the old one would permit
them to halt for siesta and refreshment as there
was no other such shelter from the heat for
miles around. Janna nodded with i'll grace. She
saw the boy looking with admiring surprise at
Tasl and she did not want them.


Tasl's broad high-cheek-boned face was
sweetly honey -colored with sun and wind, and
the braidsof her shining hair were honey-colored
Also The heavy black lashes and sleepy black
eyes now alight with laughter we're brilliant in
their golden setting. The grandmother guessed
what the men were thinking when they ex-
changed quick significant looks. They had prob
ably argued about it riding through the fields
before sun-up watching the women at work.
There were too few beautiful Bulgarian women.
You certainly did not see them tending the
roses nor hoeing the tobacco fields. All the
travellers who stopped in Kiron we're overcome
when tney saw dSl.


What is your business?" inquired Janna
tartly.


But Tasl was smiling at the boy in her gentle,
friendly way, and he was smiling back. his
broad teeth as white as hers in his dark lively
face She moved little to make room for him
against the hospitable trunk and patted the
ground at her side, a gay young innocence in
her welcome.


The men sat down. The elder said they were
Yomi and Tomaso Davidovitch from over the
mountains. They were going into Kiron to bar
gain for the oil from the rose crop.


Tasl felt the warning pressure of her grand
mothers hand on her arm, and said they were
homeward bound from the market She gave
them water from her water cooler. No, she did
not work in the fields. More than that she
would not say.


After the four had slept through the MONDAY
heat, Tasl rose and prepared the oxcart for her
grandmother. 'She cannot walk, 3" she explained
to the travellers as she stopped to raise Janna.


Yomi leaped to his feet LET me" he said,
and lifted the light little body to the dusty
cushions. Tasl smiled her thanks, fixed up the
big yellow umbrella and climbed onto the cart.

BY WILLIAM K. HUTCHINSON


Q.N.SO The seventy-fifth Con-
gress roared down the adjourn
ment trail today with leaders
fighting to block every move that
might interfere with final enact
ment of President Roosevelt'S
legislative program.


Final obstacle to adjournment
appeared to be the sugar quota
bill. now before the Senate
Finance Committee, which the
administration opposes in its pres
ent form. The House imposed
quotas on the importation of re-
fined sugar from Puerto Rico and
Hawaii over the objections Of the
Interior Department.


Veto Threats Voiced


Administration leaders hoped to
strike out these limitations in the
Senate, but leaders of the sugar
bloc predicted they would be re-
tanned. This brought threats of
veto from the President, in which
event the sugar bloc leaders be-
lieved they could enact the bill
over the Presidents objections.


Meanwhile, after six months OF
bitter controversy, the Senate dis
posed of President RooSevelt'S Su-
preme Court enlargement bill by
sending to the House q revised
substitute measure for procedural
reforms in the lower Federal
courts. The high court would not
be affected. The bill was passed
without a record vote under the
guidance of Vice President Garner.


Both Sides Approve


Both Senator Ashurst CD of
Arizona, Judicial Committee chair
man, who led the losing fight for
the Presidents original bill, and
Senator Wheeler CD OF Mon
tana, leader of the opposition,
approved the bill.


Two oCner important aQmln1SCra-
ton bills, already passed by the
Senate, we're pending in the House.
These were the mild wage-hour
bill and the emaSculated Wagner
Housing act.


Modification Talked


There was wild talk in House
corridors Of modifying all three
bills in keeping with White House
wishes. Administration leaders
were putting a soft pedal" on
amendments and hoping to obtain
House approval of the Senate bills,
practically unchanged, to avoid
further legislative controversies
that might extend the present ses-
sion indefinitely.


The sugar bill, anti-lynching
legislation and the government re-
organization bill, providing six
new secretaries for the President,
were pending in the Senate after
passing the House. Prompt action
was promised on the sugar bill.

Disturbing reports have been re-

in remote Rossel Island cannibalism
is being revived Recently the island
ers began to study the English Ian
guage and gave evidence that the
ways of the white men were making
themselves felt. English explorers,
however have found signs on the
island indicating that cannibalism is
being practiced again in the wilder
parts. There is some doubt that it
ever was wholly stamped out. Rossel
Island was once the scene of the
worst cannibal outrage ever known,
more than 800 Chinese shipwrecked
on their way to Australia being slain
and devoured.

Until recently. most well-informed
Americans supposed that medical science
had finally conquered yellow fever Be-
ginning with Gorgas, Reed and their
confreres in Havana, science had shown
that the disease was transmitted solely
by one particular species of mosquito,
called aeges aegypti; as this obnoxious
pest was brought under control, yellow
fever was sure to vanish.


The annual report of the Rockefeller
Foundation, however, reveals that the
picture is not so rosy. For it has been
discovered that yellow fever can and
does occur in regions where aedes aegypti
has never appeared. Vast areas of South
American jungle are centers of the dis
ease. and some entirely new villain must
be sought.


There are no brighter chapters in all
medical history than those which tell
of its fight with yellow fever. 1t may
be discouraging to learn that the fight
has not yet been won, but has merely
entered new phase. And yet, in view
Of past performances, who can doubt
that medical science will find the brains,
the courage and the stick-to- -itiveness to
carry on until the victory is final?

NEW YORK, May 8-Commodity
prices continued to spiral downward
this week, although there was less
unanimity to the decline than at any
time since it started early in April.


Changes were narrow In most in
stances. Stand-out exceptions, how
ever, were coffee and steel scrap. The
former swept up on private reports
from Brazil that approximately 10
per cent Of the current crop would be
destroyed. Thus despite big harvest,
brokers saw smaller exports a distinct
possibility.


The steel scrap picture has been
changed, dealers said, by the heavy
supplies brought into the market when
the price jumped above $23 a ton
several weeks ago. At that time there
was a genuine scarcity Of the waste
metal, but the high price being Of
fered caused scrap dealers to scour
the countryside for supplies.


Prices Drop Farther.


Since then quotations have been
shaved is per cent, increased offerings
combined with a slight dip in steel
mill activity being held responsible.


The Associated Press weighted index
Of IS important commodities slid to
9l.98 per cent OF the 1926 average
from 92.5l last week, and compared
with 72,44 year ago.


There were IA declines among
staples making up the index, while
gained and II were unchanged.


Yielding to pressure exerted by
heavily weighted steel scrap. industrial
commodities fell back Other reactions
included hides, tin and burlap. Rub
Der, bituminous coal and turpentine
picked up slightly.


Live stock and food groups were
higher. Hogs strengthened as stocks
dwindled and the outlook cleared for
smaller marketings this Summer This
advance was sufficient to offset lower
cattle and lamb quotations. Sugar and
flour improved with coffee, while eggs,
cocoa and lard gave ground.


Farm Staples Mixed.


Although corn and cotton managed
to maintain the rising trend begun a
few weeks back, weakness in wheat,
oats and rye was potent enough to
drop the index.


Operating at the highest sustained
level since the war, the textile in
dustry is nevertheless reported to have
built up larg inventory backlog.
This has resulted In constant
whiting away at the price structure.
The latest decline in cotton cloth and
silk carried the index to the lowest

VIENNA, February 13 R.-Ed-
ward. Duke Of Windsor, who gave
up the British throne for love, today
met the honeymooning heiress to
another throne, Crown Princess
Juliana Of the Netherlands, and her
new husband, Prince Bernhard.


Shortly before he bade a fearful
farewell to his sister Mary, the Prin-
cess Royal, Edward Unexpectedly met
Juliana in the dining room of the
Bristol Hotel.


The Duke gave Juliana an impulsive
embrace and chatted with her for
10 minutes, mostly about skiing, Of
which both are devotees.


Both Princess Mary and her brother
were deeply moved when they parted
at the Vienna station, ending a weeks
visit. The Princess hid her grief in
o bouquet Of roses and violets the
former British monarch had given
her, while many Of the women on
lockers wept.


Edward showed anger when motion
picture cameramen attempted to
record the scene. Police conhscated
the cameras.


Princess Mary and her husband,
the Earl Of Harewood, journeyed back
toward London bearing gifts from the
voluntarily-exile Duke to his mother.

SAN FRANCISCO May 15.-A ST.
100000 flreproof, earthquake proof
and robbery-proof mint on a solid
rock foundation, was dedicated here
today.


The streamlined, flve-story build
ing overlooks the central business dis
trict from rocky knoll, and soon
will replace the historic downtown
mint as the Governments West Coast
coinage center.


Mrs. Nellie Tayloe Ross, director Of
all the Nations minis, was asked to
make the dedicatory address this aft
ernoon in the presence OF State and
city officials and hundreds of San
Franciscans, who then may inspect
the structure for first and probably
last time.


The building, under construction
for 20 months, commands the corner
Of Market and Buchanan streets like
fortress.


Every possible means, both scientific
and massive, has been taken to pro-
tect the mint's precious metals from
robbers. The building, however, was
not constructed to withstand a war
time attack. Its roof is not bomb
proof and there are no grills across
tall windows.


Huge 22-ton doors protect vaults
with 2-foot reinforced concrete walls,
so strengthened with steel bars that
difficulty was experienced in pouring
the cement


The vault doors are equipped with
one time lock and two combination
locks. No employe knows both combi-
nations


Should a robber get into one of
the vaults, his troubles would begin.
Mlcrophones in the ceiling would
transmit any noise he made to the
central guard room. 1t has a tWo-way
radio connection with police head
quarters and, in case of serious trouble,
with the preside, where some 800
Army Regulars are stationed.


Giant air suction apparatus has been
installed in the refining and coinage
rooms to conduct dust-laden air to q
separator which cost s65,0OO. 1t is
expected to pay for itself in two
years through recovered gold dust.

Federal wild game officials have an
nounced proudly that an albino bison
calf has been born on the national
bison refuge near Missoula, Mont.


Stanley P. Young OF the Bureau OF
Biological Survey said q pure white
bison was a rarity in tho animal
kingdom.


Young said an albino bison calf was
born four years ago, and when ma
tured it was segregated from the herd
with several cows. The white bull
mated with his mother and the Sec
ond albino calf, female, was born
several days ago.


Young said that white bison were
rare even in the days when countless
thousands of the native buffalo roamed
the plains. He said the Indians re-
garded the albino bison as big medi-
cine" and that the lucky hunter who
killed one WAS assured success.


Young said the new albino calf and
its father were the only white bison
in the herd OF the Biological Survey,
which now numbers about 1000 head.

dered sugar. On the platter you

cake. Now turn out the mold

HOUSTON, Tex, April l2.-Tennis


stars seem to be having trouble
finishing their jobs this season, and
the seventh annual River Oaks tour
ney, which featured Bryan (Bitsy)

each team had won one set.

pm. today.

ing the River Oaks tourney to win the
Atlanta, Ga, doubles title from Bob
Riggs and Joe Hunt of Los Angeles.
That match was rained out at Atlanta
two weeks ago. Grant and Sabin will
meet for the Atlanta tournament
singles at Atlanta next Sunday.

NEW YORK, March 2O.-Heavy
pressure on United States Govern
ment loans most of the week, together
with plentiful supply of high-grade
corporates, combined to lower prices
in the bond market


The chief influences producing this
result were a growing expectation of
higher money rates, official intima-
tlons of fears of runaway price levels
and the opinion of some that Federal
loans were out of line with high-grade
corporate and municipal bond prices.


The so-called buyers strike of large
institutional investors has been laid
to their belief that higher yields are
indicated by the money markets pres
ent trend. Financial circles agree
that insurance companies and COM
mercial banks, particularly the smaller
interior institutions have stood aloof
from the bond market in recent weeks.
The latter were said to be among the
more active sellers of Government and
high-grade corporate obligations dur
ing the latest period.


Warnings by three Federal officials
that rising commodity and other
prices might, unless checked, get out
of control also fitted into the senti-
ment operating for the downside
Such a situation, investment circles
pointed out, would leave bondholders
with fixed income mediums at time
when the purchasing power of the
dollar was shrinking


Railroad and low-yield issues were
the chief losers in the domestic cor
porate list.

NEW YORK, March 20.-Commodity
prices continued to push into new high
ground last week, although there was
less unanimity to the swing than has
been evident in the past month or
longer.


Live stock, industrial and agricultural
staples chalked up new peaks for the
year, while recently soaring non-fer-
rouS metals were set back after climb
ing 35 per cent since the turn of the
year.


The Associated Press weighted index
OF 35 important wholesale commodities
rose to 1886 per cent of the 1925 aver
age, the highest level in seven years,
from 94.69 a week ago and compared
with 74.40 in the same period last year.


Demand for raw materials was heavy
as industrial activity doomed to the
best rate since late 1929. Steel scrap
jumped to a 14-year tor with coke for
the production of pig iron scarce.


Lumber Prices Raised.


Lumber quotations were marked up
a notch. Strikes in West Coast mills,
following on the heels of the long mari
time strike, reduced available supplies
in the face of rising building activity.
Hides, rubber and linseed oil also ad-
vanced.


Lead was unable to hold gains of re-
cent weeks, dropping about 10 per cent.
Leaders in the trade held speculation
abroad had driven prices too high. Tin
gave ground before the same selling
wave that hit lead.


Products of the farm were sharply
higher, reports showing insufficient
moisture. From the four quarters of
the world demand for grains was
strong-corn, wheat and rye sharing
the upturn. Oats weakened slightly.


Cotton Trend Erratic.


Cotton swung erratically, jumping
one-half cent pound and later losing
most of the gain.


With livestock herds depleted by two
droughts in three years, hogs, cattle
and lamb were marked up.


Foods were mixed. Eggs and butter
improved, sugar and lard dipped. Tex
tiles advanced under the leadership
Of wool and silk.

By the Associated Press.


Thousands of grown-ups who re-
member the little red school house"
with its pot-bellied stove and back
breaking benches will be introduced to
the modern American school when
their children return to class during
the next few weeks.


Public Works Administration ex-
perts, who have scanned plans for
4,493 schools built with P. w. A. as
sistance in the last four years, say
revolutionary changes are being made
in educational buildings. Many Of
these are to improve ventilation and
sanitary, heating and lighting facil-
tiles.


Indirect lighting and air. conditioned
heating systems are being installed
widely. Insulated roofs and walls ere
used increasingly, and sound-proofing
is. installed where finances permit,
especially in cafeterias. The familiar
bell which changed a warning to tardy
students appears to have been sup
planted by electric hall gongs, sirens,
and class room buzzers.


Radio and moving picture apparatus
and amplifying systems are in many
new schools. A Providence (R. H.
high school, four stories high, safe
guards its self-operating elevators for
teachers and crippled children with
an electric eye.


School room windows turn inside out.
Desk tops adjust upward like artists
eases to prevent eyestrain and i'm
prove posture. School seats may be
adjustable or form fitting.


Some schools are equipped to give
all students shower baths twice weekly
by use Of horseshoe-shaped spray
rooms through which pupils pass in
rapid succession.


There are more swimming pools
with water chemically treated and
light treated. In some buildings stu
dents step in a germicidal solution
before entering the pool or shower.
Gymnasiums are combined with
auditoriums in grade schools. Many
new high schools have two-one for
boys and one for girls. The new high
schools separate them from audi
toriums, however, and build the latter
with sloping floors and stage equip
ment.

The Lodge was more imposing than
usual in the storm. 1t was formidable
structure of hewn cypress logs. and it
typified the wealthy mans idea of
rough dwelling. Judith knew what the
inside was like: door opening onto a
huge room resplendent with hunting
trophies. There was fireplace oppo-
site the door, and on each side OF it,
facing each other. two luxurious
lounges There we're easy chairs scat
tered about and small rugs which, in
the winter, were rolled back for infor
NAL dancing on pre-hunting nights.
And way off to the right was the
dining room and beyond that the
modern. tiled kitchen. Near the din
ing room door was fight of steps
leading to a gallery running the en-
tire breadth of the Lodge. Onto this
balcony opened dozen bedrooms
where the members slept at night on
their hunting excursions.


The vista, as one entered the front
door. was artistic and impressive.
Fireplace. leather couches. reading
lamps, and second floor which, to the
eye, was simply long balcony studded
with doors. In the winter there was
always fire of oak logs blazing
merrily. But tonight there would be
no fire: nothing but brief respite from
the storm.


Alan stretched out his hand toward
the door. and Judith stopped him.
Isn't this rather senseless, Alan?"


Talking it out with Bruce? No
ma am - it most definitely isn't"


He opened the heavy oak door and
they stepped into the dim yellow light
Alan closed the door behind them.
and they stood for a brief instant,
silently. Then she heard the young
mans voice. Alan said. Good Lordr'


She looked up at his face. 1t was
gray and strained He said, STEADY.
Judith. steady"


She followed the direction Of his
eyes, and pressed her fingers against .
her lips to stifle scream.


The couch at the left of the fire.
place, at right angles to the long wall,
was empty. But on the rug before it
was something - the figure Of man
sprawled face forward on the floor.
The left hand was stretched out as
though toward the fireplace, the right
hand was underneath; the figure was
bent at the waist, knees drawn up. A
haC and a raincoat had been flung
across the end table near the couch.


Judith stood motionless, terrified.
as Alan moved swiftly across the
room. Despite the August heat, she
shivered as though with chill. She
watched him as he knelt beside the
figure. Then, without rising, Alan
turned his face in her direction.


"Your husband" he said quietly.
has been murdered"

CORDOBA FRONT, March 2s.-Ma-
neuvering behind screen OF crack
Moorish cavalrymen, two wings OF the
southern insurgent army launched a
simultaneous attack today to smash
the government barrier to the rich
mining country OF Cuidad Real.


The perfectly synchronized drive
eastward against Pozoblanco and
northward up the valley Of the Por-
cuna River shattered an Easter Sun

The signal for the general advance

weather as it was relayed from noun
tain peak to mountain peak where

had been plotting the position of gov
eminent troops throughout the week
end.


AS the Moorish cavalry trouble
ahooters" crashed into action in the
mountainous terrain Of Cordoba Prov
ince, the infantry squads spread out
into skirmish order behind them.


From the heights, the observers di-
rected the advance, spotting enemy
held artillery positions, machine gun
nests and troop movements, and relay
ing the information to the front lines
on the lower slopes.


Would Pinch Of Vast Area


The eastward moving column laid its
course roughly along the position Of
the prickly spine of the Sierra Mo-
rena Range while Gen. Gon2alo
Queipo de Llano's northernmost COL
umn pushed upward along the valley
of the Porcuna.


The double thrust aimed along the
northern and eastern edges of box
like area, IS miles on a side, and II
successful, would mean the pinching
off OF vast area On the southern
front.


The advance spread from the Sec
tors about Cordoba, Pozoblanco and
Purcuna to virtually all sections OF
the southern front in unit engage
ments stretching all the way from the
Taglls River, 80 miles south of Madrid,
to the Mediterranean, 230 miles away.


Loyalists Defeated.


On the extreme southern sector, to
the east of captured Malaga, severe
defeat with heavy losses was inflicted
when a government attack on the
= Orgiva area was turned into a rout.


It was the first attack in force by
the government army since the occu-
patton of Malaga scattered their
coastal columns.


Sweeping down from widely sepa-
rated positions on the southern slopes
Of the Sierra Nevada range, they
clashed Unexpectedly with insurgent
Yihemen and machine -gunners, man
ming strongly fortified line.


Insurgent officers said the govern
ment commanders had apparently been
led to believe the sector was abandoned.


Pressing the advantage gained from
surprise, insurgent cavalry took up the
attack and pursued the retreating gov
eminent troops back into the noun
tains.


Squads of infantrymen followed close
behind, consolidating the new posi-
tions.

The answer, we'll informed circles

German Air Minister Hermann Goer-
ing concludes his visit to Italy this
week end.


The conversations between Goering
and Premier Mussolini, these sources
said, formed the basis for the joint
Italo- German policy which the Italian
note will set forth.


Italy and Germany, they reiterated,

to the nations of Europe because they
were considered purely private ques-

HANDING yourself beauty as you
bridge the seasons isn't exactly
an easy task. There are all the hand
marks of an active, sporting Sum-
mer -. a deep coat Of tan, no doubt,
which is no longer fashionable this
Fall rough skin, broken cuticle. split
nails, callous spots from maneuvering
oars or tennis rackets.


The first thing to do is to soften
the hands. Here's an excellent treat
ment: First, cleanse your hands thor
oughly. Instead of using your usual
soap, try pore cleanser in the form
Of soap-substitute grains. Moisten the
skin, wash with the grains and rinse
thoroughly. You'll find that the lit
tie dead cells, or scarf skin, are readily
removed and the hands are left look
ing so much lighter, cleaner and
softer.


Then apply your cuticle cream to
the cuticle and your hand lotion to
the skin, massaging in firm, rotary
movement.


One of New York's most famous
experts in hand care and nail color
has developed several exercises which
she calls gymnastics for hands to
give them grace and glamour. One
is called the piano player: Place
hands on table, with fingers touching
dc
separately five times, holding the
other fingers firmly ON the table.


Another: Hold hands out, palms
down; keep them perfectly relaxed,
then swing them around in circles
from wrist, clockwise and counter
clockwise. Repeat 10 times.


Third: Grasp left hand firmly with
right hand and rotate at wrist clock
wise and counter clockwise 10 times.
Repeat on other hand.


Fourth: Make q tight fist, fling
fingers out, fan shape; then relax COM
pletely. Repeat each hand 10 times.


Fifth: Bend hand at wrist, holding
fingers backward ~ far a. possible:
dip fingers down, initiating the dive
OF swan, and move forward, con-
tinuing the motion. Repeat each hand
10 times.


This expert returned recently from
an extended trip to England. She
says: "One thing strikes me particu-
larly in comparing English hands with
our American hands: The English
woman holds her hands beautifully in
respose, whereas here the art of
gesture is paramount. Repose VS.. rest
lessness." Something to think about
and practice.

The Air Commerce Bureau, in a

sponsible.


Bad weather was given as con-

range reception was a factor in the

death.

turning back to make on instrument

Lake George and vicinity, in ad-

The American youngster. from a
sports standpoint, is the most fortu-
nate in the world.


No other nation furnishes its youth
as we'll as adults, with such oppor-

Sporting equipment costs less than

Take to American Attitude.

many years before.


Physical education is major point

sums are spent to assure physical
training for all youths. Sports par
ticipation is emphasized in the army
as never before.


Many swimming pools, gymnasia
and stadia have been built by the
government. Huge amounts were ex-
pended to build stadia for the Olympic
Games at Berlin last Summer. And
these now will serve for important
sports exhibitions. The Olympic

In sports among German boys and
girls.

tress Of the screen today, Paul
NUM- and Miriam Hopkins are

Curiously enough, although both

fore that we're outstanding In

AN EXCELLENT CAST


The two favorites have had
widely different backgrounds but
both reached their goals along a
parallel path. Mum, born in Aus
tria, was the son Of q theatrical
family and made his first appear
ance before the footlights as q
mere child while travelling with
his parents, making his way to
prominence in the New York
theater for his striking character
izationS.


Miss Hopkins was the daughter
Of a DISTINGUISHED Georgia family,
and was educated in various East
ern schools, starting her acting
career in. student plays, and reach
ing Broadway fame by way OF bal.
let dancing, vaudeville, musical
comedy and dramatic roles.


Both were for years among the
foremost stars Of the Theater
Guild and other art theater groups
in New York, MUM was the first
to enter pictures, coming to Holly
wood early in 1929 to make his
screen debut in 1.-THE Valiant"
while Miss Hopkins first faced q
camera the following year in Fast
and Loose" made at q Long Island
studio.


MUNI-HOPKINS STAR


Neither was satisfied with their
initial film efforts but both have
climbed to tremendous heights of
popularity with their subsequent
performances, MUM in 1.-THE Story
Of Louis Pasteur," in which film
he won the Academy Award,
''Black Fury" CDR. Socrates" and
the recent success The Good
Earth" and Miss Hopkins in such
pictures as "These Three" Bar
barry Coast" and "Splendor."


In their new picture, 'The
Woman Love-" the two have per.
haps the most dramatic roles Of
their careers. Num- portrays a
shy, sensitive, wartime fher, un-
popular with his fellows and bitter
over his own failings. Miss Hop
ktns' has the role of Muni's wife,
q woman who has never known
what love was until she falls sud-
denly and irrevocably in love with
a young aviator who, as she learns
too late, becomes Muni's closest
friend at the front.


The gripping situations that
arise make the film an unusually
powerful one, and afford both
stars, as well as Louis Hayward,
who portrays the youthful flyer,
exceptional dramatic opportuni-
ties. Colin Give, Wally Albright,
Mady Christians, Paul Guilfoyle,
Owen Davis, jr., Adrian Morris
and other notable players are in
the supporting cast.


Anatole Litvak directed the AL
bert Lewis production, with Ethel
Borden and Anthony WELLER writ
ing the screen play from the best
selling novel by Joseph Kessel.

The services will be on a scale ex-

The British New York Bermuda
plane, christened the Cavalier" has
a top speed of about 200 miles an hour
as compared to 100 for the Sikorsky
Bermuda Clipper" But probably the
most interesting comparison between
the two craft is that the American ship
carries twenty four passengers to the
British planes twelve. And this de-
spite the fact that each has roughly
the same horsepower. Yet the
Empire" flying boats were brought
out after the original Sikorsky Clip
pers we're already in service.


The British have had little ocean
flying experience and view the
Bermuda New York run as valuable
training ground. For Pan American
oceans hold no novelty. In addition to
its Pacific record, which includes we'll
over hundred crossings of the worlds
greatest ocean without single mis-
hap, it has made more than 1900
flights across the Caribbean since the
opening of its Jamaica-Colombia route
in 1881.


That 6OO-mile run is comparable to
the New York Bermuda hop, so the
new Atlantic service means nothing
more to the American company than
transferring a ship and providing the
necessary ground facilities.


A complete flying boat base was
constructed by the British some time
ago on Darrell's Island in Hamilton
Harbor, Bermuda. This is being used
by the American company, which is
supplying similar accommodations for
the British at its temporary Port
Washington base on Long Island. Pan
American also has arranged for even
tual terminal facilities at Baltimore
and Charleston, S. c., for use when
weather forbids operating direct into
New York. These facilities will be
shared with Imperial Always and
other foreign operators who will furnish
similar service to Pan American IN
their respective countries.


The first piece of the Atlantic is
an accomplished fact; and before long
passengers who want to fly all the way
across may have their wishes gratified.

we'll One leg had been torn away.

and local police and volunteers had
conducted since Helens hat, shoes
and books were found beside the
Coatesville-M -Modena road, along which

ment related that he killed the
girl with his truck and stripped her
clothes from her and attacked her
after she was dead, an autopsy IN
dicated she might have been living
when she was dropped into the
well.

MANILA, April 12.-Filipino con-
staoularymen today sought to clean
up a Moro rebellion in Lanao Prov
lnce which already has claimed at
least % lives.


Three hundred soldiers captured the
most important stronghold of the
hery Mohemmedan fighters Sunday
after a six-hour attack, during which
mortars were used to demolish the log
fort at Makaguiling, on the Island of
Mindanao.


Two Moros were killed, and two
others were wounded in the fight. Two
soldiers were wounded, advices re-
ceived from the capital of the prov
lnce by Maj. Gen. Pauline Santos.
chief of the constabulary staff, dis
closed.


Gen. Santos ordered the troops to
pursue the escaping Moros.


Last week the soldiers used cannon
to dlslodge rebellious tribesmen from
several other forts.


Though firearms are banned by law,
some Of the Mohammedans are sup
Piled with them, and have faunted
them before island police.


The Moros and Filipinos from the
northern part of the Archipelago are
traditional enemies, but the present
uprising apparently resulted from the
MoroS' opposition to compulsory mill
tary training, taxation, possibility Of
