Legislation designed to provide debt
ridden wage earners relief from bill
collectors. threats of suit and garnish-
ment processes came before the House
today.


Under the Chandler bankruptcy bill,
which sponsors hope to get through
Congress before adjournment, such
wage earners could go into Federal
courts and obtain assistance in settle
ment Of their obligations.


The court would call creditors to-
gether and work out plan whereby
the debtor could settle out of his future
earnings over two-year period.


The bill slashes costs which now
render bankruptcy laws unworkable for
wage earners. 1t also would permit
the debtor to pay those costs on the
installment plan.


The legislation also carries provi-
sions designed to eliminate grave
abuses" which the Securities and Ex-
change Commission reported in recent
Investigations of corporate reorganiza-
ton proceedings in bankruptcy courts


Those Investigations showed, the
commission said, that in reorganization
ventures the inside few" usually in
vestment bankers and the corporation
management, benefited by sacrificing
the interests of scattered, unorganized
investors


The bill would give the courts ad-
ministrative and expert assistance in
dealing with reorganization cases.

Perfect weather. clear and crisp,
vas expected to be Dame Natures
contribution to Washington's most
elaborate Halloween festival and
parade tonight.


Anticipating that the witches and
goblins that walk around have noted
the festive occasion is being cele-
brated a day early and have timed
their annual appearance accordingly.
the colorful pageant of gigantic comic
figures, floats, bands and coStumed
marchers has been scheduled to get
under way at 1880 O'Clock.


Thousands of persons are expected
to line up along the parade route on
Constitution avenue NV. between
Fourth and Seventeenth streets.
Late this afternoon an elaborate sys-
tenn of traffic control will be put
into effect to prevent downtown traf-
fic jams and to expedite persons 60
ing to and from the parade.


Reception Opens Festivities.


The initial event of the evening
will be q reception at the Willard
Hotel for the District Commissioners
and the mayors and other officials of
towns and cities in nearby Mary
land and Virginia, who will review
the parade as guests of honor.


Spectators will be treated 20 a
pageant which will include 10 huge,
inflated balloon figures representing
animals, dozen or more bands and
bugle corps, many civic and CONNER
cial floats, decorated private vehi-
cles, costumed group ana individual
marcher's humorous skits.


The Halloween queen, Miss Betty
Virginia Lewis, 18-year-old Temple
School student, will meet the mem
bers of her court at the Willard Ho-
tel before the parade. Then they
will lead the line of march as far
MS the court of honor, between Fiji
teenth and Seventeenth streets NV,
and then watch the remainder of
the parade.


The parade will pass the review
ing stand directly opposite the court
of honor. Here will be seated the
Commissioners, visiting mayors, men,
bers of the diplomatic corps and
other distinguished guests.


Metropolitan and park police de-
tails will be reinforced by National
Guard officers and Boy Scouts in
handling traffic and looking out for
the safety of spectators and marchers.


Judges Named.


The Halloween Committee, which
has been working on details of the
celebration for several weeks, held
its final meeting yesterday with Gen.
eral Chairman Harry p Somerville.
1t was announced the following per-
sons will act as judges to decide the
winning divisions and individuals:
Charles e. Kurtzman, costumed indi-
vidual marchers; George Lohr, COM
mercial floats; George Thompson,
civic floats; Mabel Mehaffey, decorated
private vehicles; James M. Thur
mond, bands, and Anne Abbott, cos
tuned group marchers.


The judges will not announce their
decision until Monday. The COM
mittee members felt that would give
the judges more time to reach their
decisions and would eliminate the
congestion which would accompany
announcement of awards Immediately
after the parade.


MIR. Somerville also announced the
queen and members of her court will
be guests of the Raleigh Hotel at a
dinner dance Monday night.


The queens division of the parade
will include Maurice Jarvis, the King
Of Halloween; Dennis Connell, jester;
David Cole and Roy Burton, heralds,
and Jack Exline and Andrew Jack
son, pages.

BIRMINGHAM, Ala, October 16.-
A terrific explosion killed SO hope
lessly trapped men deep in Mulga
coal mine near Birmingham early
today


Rescue crews battled heroically
through smoke and dangerous gases to
bring out the blackened and mutilated
bodies.


Only one elbow of the mine was
affected. and the remaining $50
workers at Mulga shuddered as they
contemplated how narrowly their lives
had been spared. If the blast haG
occurred near the mine entrance, all
would have been trapped.


Mangled, burned and battered, the
bodies were brought up from the
depths on coal cars. Approximately
800 spectators. including distraught
wives, children and parents, watched
the grim proceedings in horror.


The detonation was heard in Sec
tlons OF Birmingham, more than IL
miles from the scene. Fire Marshal
Sam Williams blamed coal gas for
the blast.


Reaches Fellow Workers.


Forrest Kelley, miner. was first
TO reach his stricken fellow workers.


Some of them must have beer
killed by black Damp" he said
They might have been saved if they
had remained in small pocket which
was not demolished"


Many of the victims were covered
by debris and Identification was diff
cult. The grime-streaked rescue crews
pulled their torn bodies from the
Wreckage of working approximately
miles from the main entrance.


One Escapes Death.


One man, Ivan Fox, miraculously
escaped death in the blast. He suf-
fered major burns and was unable to
tell of his experience.


The bodies were taken to under
taking establishments at Bessemer. 13
miles from here, where a list of the
oedo was being computed.


R. M. Marshall, vice president of
the woodward Iron Co., operators of
the mine, said the victims were about
equally divided between white and COL
ored miners.


The bodies were brought to the sur
lace at daybreak. Homes of the miners
were deserted, but State highway pa
trolmen and Birmingham police kept
the rural roads open.


Only one telephone was available to
newspaper men and for emergency
calls, and conversations were limited
to one minute each.


In Isolated Region.


Mulga lies in an isolated, mountain
Gus region which includes the best
coal lands in Alabama. Its coal is
used primarily for iron making, being
shipped to the Woodward blast fur
naces few miles away.


First news of the disaster came from
laconic call to police headquarters
here, asking that several arnbulances
be sent, and for police to keep the
AOoO ClcdI.


Rescue crews fought their way into
the elbow despite warnings that a
trip into the mine was extremely haz-
ardous. Equipped with oxygen masks,
a squad from the United States Bureau
OF Mines led the way into the elbow
where the victims lay.


The hills about the mine shaft were
covered with frost and the cold added
to the suffering of relatives of the VIC
Tins.


This disaster was the first of major
proportions In Alabama since the
Overton blast in 1925, in which 81 lost
their lives. Mulga is only few miles
from Dolomite, where SO died in a
dust explosion in 1922.

DETROIT, Sept. THE motor
city today was assured of the
1888 gold cup race, speedboat
classic of America, after Herb
Mendelson's veteran Notre Dame
shattered two race records to win
the three heat event with a record
average speed of 63.675 miles per
hour.


The Notre Dame, piloted by
Clell Perry, defeated the Alagi,
driven by Italy's Count Theo
RoSsi, in the first and third heats
of the 90-mile event. The Italian
speedster took the cecond heat,
overtaking the Notre Dame late in
the race with a 71.466 miles per
hour lap that was the fastest of
the day.


The Notre Dame averaged
68.645 miles per hour in winning
the third and deciding heat,
breaking the old heat record of
6O.86 miles per hour.


Detroit will receive the race
next year under the gold cup
ruling that the race be staged at
the home course of the winning
boat.

HENDhYE, France, Dec. 18
QN.SJ.-Insurgent General
Frances next big offensive
against the Spanish loyalists is
due to start January 7 with the
object of capturing Barcelona,
Catalan capital and now seat Of
the leftist government.


Insurgent circles, revealing these
plans today, said they expected
Barcelona will fall" by the end

is instructing his armed forces to
spare civilians in the drive and to
respect British property.

Meanwhile, in an announce.
ment at Seville, 1nsurgent Gen.
Gueipo de Llano denied loyalist
claims that government troops
had seized any strategic positions
in the Teruel sector. He declared
insurgent troops had surrounded
so government tanks which
"crept" through the insurgent
lines in an attempt to attack them
from the rear.

word that a government defense
ministry communique claimed
loyalist troops, following up their
victorious offensive begun Wednes-
DAY, had surrounded the insur.
gent positions on the Teruel
front, cutting all communication
lines, despite a heavy snowfall. ..


VALENCIA SHELLED

an insurgent warship, for the
first time since the war began,
had succeeded in shelling Valen.
cia, causing heavy damages. Cas-
ualties were not known.


Hitherto, .Valencia's defenses
had prevented any naval lombard
ments, although the city frequent
ly has been punished by aerial At-
tacks.

eral agents. He placed himself on

Attorney General Homer Cummings
today issued the necessary papers for
the release from prison of Anthony
Tony Labrizetta. "a, and George
Sargent. 49, serving 25-year terms for
mail robbery it is claimed they did
not commit.


President Roosevelt, acting on Cum
mings' recommendation. yesterday
granted unconditional pardons to the
two men, who are residents Of Akron,
Ohio.


While Cummings report to the
President was not made public, it was
learned at the Department of Justice
that officials are convinced the crime
for which La abrizetta and Sargent were
imprisoned was committed by Alvin
Karpis, notorious kidnaper, and his
gang of bandits.


Labrizetta and Sargent were among
several suspects questioned by postal
inspectors Immediately after the SIPS
600 machine-guu robbery of a mail
truck at Warren, Ohio. on April "a,
1885. The pair was partially "identl-
fed" by witnesses. and convicted after
two trials by jury.


Throughout their period of arrest
and prosecution the men insisted they
were innocent and were the victims of
a 'frame-up" The evidence against
them admittedly was mostly circum-
stantial.


Less than seven months after the
Warren robbery similar hold-up
occurred at Garrettsville, Ohio, under
circumstances that pointed to the
same gang in each case. The second
robbery was found to be the work of
Alvin Karpis, Harry Campbell and
others Of their crowd. and this pair
confessed the Garrettsville hold-up
after their capture by Federal Bureau
of Investigation agents.


Although Karpis was noncommit-
tai regarding the Warren robbery.
subsequent investigation strength
ened the belief that the Karpis gang.
and not Labrizetta and Sargent, was
responsible.


Cummings acted on the advice of
Pardon Attorney Daniel Lyons, who
made thorough study of the case.

SHARKS teeth, some as large as a


mans hand, are the only known
remains of giant sharks that ruled
the seas millions of years ago. Great
numbers of these fossils are found in
sandy deposits along the Atlantic
Coast and in the Pacific Ocean. Yet
few landlubbers or mariners ever see
them.


In the Chesapeake Bay region Boy
Scouts stage novel Sharks Tooth
Hunt" every Summer. Prizes are
awarded to boys who find the most,
the tiniest and the largest teeth. Dur
ing recent contest a Scout collected
over 600 teeth in one week The
shores and steep cliffs yield these
sharp, fat, age-blackened fossils.
Beach mixers dig into the hillsides
and often uncover fine specimens
Along the waters edge collectors find
the teeth washed down by rain and
wind.


Some are worn smooth by the ele-
ments and others have jagged edges.
It is surprising to find the remains
OF these deep-sea monsters in cliffs
far above the level Of the ocean. But
scientists explain these triangular fos-
sils show that ages ago the seas COW
cred vast expanses of our present-day
land. The prehistoric teeth are found
as far inland as Washington, D. c.,
while tons of them have been hauled
from Wilmington, Del, and ground
into fertilizer.


Scientists estimate the ancient
sharks attained length of 80 feet.
Their jaws were feet across, with
several rows Of upper and lower teeth!
Imagine what formidable monsters
once lurked in the early seas! A liv-
ing relatives Of this fearful denizen
is the great white shark of today,
which grows to length of 80 feet
Yet its teeth are scarcely over an
inch long.


Although sharks are big and pow
erful, they leave behind little evidence
of their existence. After death their
cartilage framework soon disappears.

ing Morocco. The frontier was prac-
tically closed to all except foreigners.

naires-mounted strong guards around
the strife centers, especially in the
Medina area and in Fee, where the
native quarter was described as ram
pant with nationalism." French mill
tary planes helped patrol the trouble
zone.


Troops and police combined made
nearly / 900 arrests yesterday and were
busy last evening breaking up demon
strations which in many cases de-
veloped into bitter street fights.

declines woul dfollow shortly.


Charts on retail meat prices at the
Bureau of Agricultural Economics
showed they had touched seven-year
highs recently-especially for tender,
juicy steaks and savory pork chops.


The economists said high prices
were caused by droughts and business
recovery.


The decline will come, the econ

crops and protests by the public over
high costs.


They said meat prices usually are
highest about this time Of year, and
gradually taper of until early Spring,
when they turn upward.


The American Federation of Labor,
stating living costs in July were 4.3

month last year, declared workers will
be forced to lower living standard
this Fall unless their pay checks are
at least per cent larger than in 1886.


Present buying power" the fed

CHICAGO, January s.-The Win.

fornia. Los Angeles had an overnight

NEW YORK, Nov. 23.--Turkey, the

steep decline in most other basic

Thanksgiving bird, dressed for the

Associated Press daily price index of

per cent from year ago.

place, they said the turkey crop last
year was the largest ever in this coun-
try, and some extra cost was added
this season at the source to make up
for the widespread losses sustained by
growers last year because of the ab-
normal supply. Feed prices earlier this
year, furthermore, were higher than
usual.

ST. JEAN DE LUZ, France.
Sept. 9 GN.SJ.-while insurgent
troops advanced on the ASturiaS
front, reports reached here today
that extremists have taken control
of Gijon, last remaining loyalist
stronghold on the Biscay coast.


The advices said refugees from
the fallen loyalist city Of San
tander caused the greatest dis
orders, forcing Gijon police to flee
to the mountains for their lives.


CITY CAPTURED


Meanwhile, advices from Llanes,
halfway between Santander and
Gijon, said the advancing insur-
gents occupied Posada, eight miles
from Ribadesella.


At the same time three squad
rons Of insurgent planes flew over
Gijon and dropped pamphlets
warning the city's defenders not
to permit their leaders to escape.


In similar fashion, residents Of
Santander were warned that 10
loyalist militiamen would be shot
for every insurgent prisoner re-
ported executed by the govern.
ment authorities.


HEAVY FIGHTING


The insurgent advance through
the mountains was registered in
the face of stubborn loyalist re-
sistance, according to reports here.
The main fighting was being
waged all along the northern
front, with the insurgents press
ing hard all along the line and
the loyalists unleaShing fierce
counter-attacks.


Advices from Madrid claimed
1000 insurgents had been slain.


LoyaliSt claims stated Govern
ment planes repulsed insurgent
aircraft which attempted to bomb
Gijon.


Earlier, insurgent planes shot
down a French commercial plane
Of the Air Pyrennes line near
Gijon. The French craft was
brought down in a hail of ma
chine gun bullets and the lone
pilot, Abel Guidez, was burned to
death. He had taken off a few
hours previously from Biarrttz,
France.

CAIRO, ILL.,, Feb. / G.N.S3.
Cairo's zero hour is at hand.


The fate Of the city depended
on a wooden frame, three feet
high and 18 inches wide, filled
with sacks of dirt, today, as the
Ohio River rose above the 60-foot
concrete sea wall protecting Cairo
from inundation.


Grim-faced, weary rivermen pa
trolled the Notwithstanding
levee. Emergency crews sped to
bolster weak spots as the muddy
flood waters started seepin g
through or tapping over the bulk
head.


Their tension belied their spoken
confidence in the emergency bulk
head.


The river stage was 59.40 feet
early today, with the waters slowly
rising. Engineers nave pred1cted
the crest, which may not be
reached until Wednesday, will not
exceed 81 feet.


The final evacuation of the city
was being concluded today. With
one highway the only means Of
egress, Mayor August Bode or
dered the evacuation of all but
the workmen toiling on the levee.


Cairo, dry thus far while above
and below it the river has swept
over dozens of towns, is 18 feet
below the surface of the river.


A weak levee on the Cache
River, above Cairo, was being
closely guarded. Should the levee
break, the only highway still open
would be flooded and Cairo would
be isolated.

CASABLANCA, French Morocco,
October 23.-French colonial forces
were reinforced tonight to guard
against native agitation after putting
down riot of Moroccan nationalists
in the strategic northern town of
Khemisset.


Military suppression of rioters and
stern prison sentences for the leaders
stirred Moslem unrest along the vital
line from Rabat and Meknes to Fee,
beneath the towering Middle Atlas
Mountains.


Resident General Auguste Nogues,
veteran Of Add Ell Krim's 1925 Riff
rebellion, rushed to Khemisset where
planes and troops maintained patrol,
while other reinforcements were sent
to neighboring villages.


Fighting reached peak when more
than 1000 Arabs, armed with knives
and guns, attacked barricades erected
around government buildings. Troops
were rushed from Rabat, and until
they arrived 10 planes few low over
the city as warning to the rioters.


Meanwhile it was learned that the
French air force being sent to North
Africa for Fall imperial maneuvers'
had been raised from the original so
planes to more than 100. The aerial
squadrons are scheduled to begin ar
irving next week.

Forced by fire to flee from their
two small rooms in the rear of a con-
demned Government-owned dwelling
at 481 Maryland avenue southwest
shortly after midnight, an unemployed
plasterer, his wife and their six chill
dren-including 16-mcnth-old baby
faced homeless and penniless fu-
ture today.


Mrs Lawrence Coleman and her
children-Lucy. 16: Harry Lee, 12;
Albert. IL; Anna Mae, 8; Louise, 2,
and Franklin, Is months-rested in
the already-crowded home of a neigh
Dor, John Allen. while the father
sought aid in procuring food and
permanent lodging. Allen said the
Coleman's stay with him was "only
temporary" Where they will go later
neither he nor the 45-year-old father
knew.


Coleman has been out of work and
confined to his bed most of the time
during the last month, his wife said.
The little food provided for his family
has been purchased with his meager
savings and the money earned during
the few days he has had work, she
added.


Awakened about I am. by firemen,
who had been called when a blaze
was discovered in one of the un-
occupied houses next door, Coleman
rushed to the street to ask where
the fire was. Before he could get
back to his front door the flames had
spread toward his fiat.


His wife and children were removed
just before the ceiling tumbled in on
the beds. The fire then spread rapidly
to the abandoned dwelling on the other
side and within few minutes wrecked
the three houses.


The Colemans were unable to save
any of their belongings. Two of the
children were picking up scattered
pieces of soaked and charred clothing
this morning. Coleman's shoes and
the baby's nursing bottle were among
the articles destroyed.


Mrs. Frank Smith, one of the neigh
bors, said she believed the blaze was
started by some men who were drink
ing" whom she saw enter the vacant
house last night. The Fire Department
listed the origin as Undetermined"


Two alarms were sounded, the first
by Henry Fife, colored chauffeur en-
ployed by the Navy Department, who
was driving through the neighborhood.


The Treasury Department, which
has charge of the property, said the
Colemans had been ordered to vacate
by February %, when the old dwell
ing will be turned over to the National
Park Service for clearing to make way
for recreational park project.

The faunas consist OF gigantic worms
and arthropods-th latter belonging to
the same general family as the crusta-
ceans and the insects and probably in
the direct ancestral line of the trilobites.
The largest of these preCambrian
arthropods was more than ten feet long.
vertable dinosaur of the race This
creature appeared in deposits $4,000 feet
below the known lower Cambrian. There
must have been an enormous time lapse
to have permitted the accumulation Of
SO much rock formation


About three thousand feet above came
new life horizon" There are still the
enormous worms and crabs, but they are
not so crude in their structure Evolu
tion has been at work producing more
efficient creatures Then, the rock strata
indicate, there was a great glaciation-
an ice age more than half billion years
ago. The big worms and crabs couldn't
stand the cold. They had enjoyed easy
living too long. With the end of the ice
another fauna appears-dwarfed crea-
lures of the same kinds. They probably
had pulled through because they didn't
require so much to eat.


Among these, the Australian paleon-
tologists believe, may be found the actual
remote ancestors of the trilobtes and of
the cepha alopods the giant creatures who
succeeded the crab-like forms AS masters
OF creation. The dwarfed fauna is still
far below the lower Cambrian and the
first actual trilobites.

Senate action on the bill providing

But here's what is causing brow
scratching:


The bill provides that one-half the

number of hunting licenses each
State sells. Many States, however,
have combination hunting and fish
ing license, and its going to be diff
cult to figure which were bought by
hunters only. All States may have
to start selling separate licenses

a lot Of ground and water Authori-
ties think the money was intended
for upland game and water fowl
projects, but the fur animal inter-
ests and the fishery people may de-
eide they are due for a slice, too.


I'VE may have to 60 to the Attor-

spokesman said. Maybe Congress

ticularly pleased with two provisions

ticipating States use their hunting
license money solely for wild-life pur-
poses. Some States do not now turn

commissions.


Another enables the Federal Gov
eminent to help conserve and de-
velop resident and upland game spe-
cies. Previously the Government.
with authority only over migrants, had

The passage and signing Of the bill

ernment militiamen was to solidify

positions while an advance guard Of
cavalry, aided by bombing and ma
chine cunning planes, harassed re.
treating insurgents.

sumed, and that mostly sour. Vege-
tables. especially peppers, tomatoes
and onions, are eaten raw. Fruits and
fats are avoided.


Eighty per cent Of the cases studied
used alcohol, but in moderation.

TWO things stand out from the recrimination sur
i rounding the seating of Hugo Black Justice
of the Supreme Court.


l. However deplorabIe his affilation with the Ku
Klux Klan Justice Black has established subsequent
record completely free of racial prejudice and religious
bigotry.


.. The attack on Black if carried further not only
will open old wounds, but may boomerang against
those who would protect the sancy of the Court from
the "biased" robes of the new Justice.


Mans memory is short, and there have been other
debates judicial bias


Several years ago. Justice Butler up before Senate
Judiciary Committee for confirmation Justice of the
Supreme Court, gave promise, through his senatorial
sponsors from Minnesota to refrain from participation
in railroad cases.


Mr.. Butler then the foremost railroad attorney
of his day. and the entire issue of railroad rates and
taxation was scheduled for review by the high bench
upon which he to take his seat. Justice Butler
took that seat, and since then has not hesated to
view railroad cases, including that of the Great
Northern Railroad. In that case, Justice Butler not
only did not step aside but had far forgot his prom
ise to the Senate Judiciary Committee that he, him
self, wrote the opinion refunding $1oOooOOO to his
old client.


More recently, Justice Roberts handed down the
opinion in the Chesapeake and Potomac Telephone
case company affiliated with the Bell Telephone


Company. Mr.. Roberts, former d-


rector in the latter company, not only
''O' ~ did not step aside, but decreed that
its affiliate entitled to important rate reductions.
Nor has Mr. Hughes stepped aside when the Standard
Oil Company and others of his old clients before
the Court which he presided Chief Justice.
The fact is that few big enough to be considered
as material for the highest bench have failed to acquire
prejudices-personal, economic or socal-which at
time other may not dsqualify them to sit
Justice of the Supreme Court.


Justice Black averages with his associates in this
respect. He may average higher. For he has come
long way since the opportunist days of his member
p,u,l u ship in the Klan.


From unknown, poor white family


S0 in Alabama he became power in the
United States Senate-a prosecutor of corruption,
crusader for equitable rights for working men
and women.


However men may have disagreed with his creed,
none have doubted his courage, his honesty or his
liberal viewpoint.


On this record, rather than act Of political ex-
pediency fifteen years ago. should his right to sit
the Supreme Court be Judged.


The debate of the last three weeks will put Justice
Black his mettle, should make him fairer, wiser
judge. But there has been enough debate. Let him
take his seat.

To the Editor Of The Star:


take your recent editorial as mani
festation of the interest of the people
in your section of the country in the
Philippines. I presume that your read
ers are proud of the splendid work done
in the Philippines by the United States.


Although the American chapter in Phil
ippine history may end in the near future,
the Filipinos wish to continue to have
friendly, cultural and economic rela-
tions with the great American people,
who have been their unselfiSh teachers
for almost 40 years. The United States
has made her impress upon the Filipinos
SO deeply that even Philippine political
independence can never wipe out her
tremendous influence. American civil
ization and democracy have rooted in
the Philippines and are there to stay.


If and when independence finally
comes I hope that the American people
will find no necessity for ending the
mutually beneficial United States
Philippine trade relations. The compile
mentary economy between your country
and mine has brought tremendous ad-
vantages and large benefits to Americans
and Filipinos. QUINTIN PAREDES.

By the Associated Press.


Seamen on Government operated
merchant vessels which enter danger
zones" in Chinese and Spanish waters
will get a $50 bonus for the extra
hazard.


TheMaritime Commission approved
the bonus last night. Maritime union
leaders affiliated with the Committee
for Industrial Organization had sug-
gested a $3.50 bonus.


The commission defined the affected
areas as:


l. Territorial waters of Spain.
Spanish Morocco and the Balearic
Islands, including waters between the
Balearic Islands and the Spanish
mainland.


z. The Yellow Sea and the East
China Sea, including all those waters
between Korea. Japan, the Riukiu
Islands, Formosa and the Chinese
mainland, north of both, excluding
Hong Kong.


Advised to Use Caution.


Recognizing the danger to neutrals
IN the waters surrounding the scenes
OF the Spanish War and the unde-
clared Sino-Japanese conflict. the
Navy several weeks ago advised all
American vessels to proceed with eau
tion.


Ships Of only two Government
operated lines ordinarily might enter
the danger zone. They are:


The American Pioneer, which oper-
ates through the Mediterranean Sea
to India via the Suez Canal, and from
the Panama Canal to ports in the Far
East and Australia.


The American France, which carries
general cargo and some passengers
from the United States to French
ports.


Maritime unionstS indicated they
would seek to win bonus payments
from private operators as we'll as from
the Federal Government. They have
contended $3.50 is a fair bonus, on the
ground that steamship lines charge
extra rates for cargoes consigned 20
ports in the danger zones.


The Maritime Commission bonus is
in addition to the insurance protec-
ton which seamen of Government
operated vessels already have as Fed
eral employees.


Should such seamen be interned in
a foreign port, the commission ruled,
their pay will continue during intern
ment.

today droned over the village Of

disorders.


Authorities estimated more than a

The trouble began last evening
when Moslems. gathered for prayers
at the Khemisset Mosque. were ad-

orators who. police said came from
Fez to organize a demonstration.


The Nationalists. singing native
Moroccan songs and carrying the
Moroccan flag, marched through the
streets. bowling over police dispatched
to halt them.


They pushed against barricades
erected before the Civil Government
Building. Police fired several times on
the Nationalists, but were unable to
disperse them.


Fierce fighting broke out on the

defenders until the French Legion
naires arrived from Rabat.


Magistrates swiftly sentenced those
arrested from 10 DAYS to year in
prison and rushed them to Rabat fol-
lowing reports that trouble was spread
ing in other towns.


Fighting reached its peak when a
mob of more than 1000 Arabs. many
of them armed with knives and guns
firing homemade bullets, attacked gov
ernment buildings.

fighting. with native Moghzani in
fantrymen and cavalrymen armed with
sabers, supported by European civil
ianS.

from Rabat. Motorized units of the
African Chasseurs arrived during the
night. Ten military planes flew low
over the city until a company of
Foreign Legionnsires was brought in
to patrol the streets.


Police and troops were sent to many
surrounding villages.

consider the Sultan Of Morocco power
less under the French protectorste,

The Agriculture Department heard
yesterday that four years of expert
ments have convinced the German
Government that it cannot become
entirely independent of foreign food
supplies.


This report came from department
observer in Berlin.


He added, however, that Germany
has made great progress toward self
sufficiency in recent years, sharply
curtailing imports of American farm
products.


Before and for a time after the
World War, Germany was the second
best world outlet for raw cotton, lard,
tobacco, grains and fruit from the
United States.


German plans, the observer said, in
clude increased raising of goats and
rabbits, partial replacement of meat
by fish, and numerous other changes
IN diet.

ton news.

sage had been discounted, most agreed.

mountain school teacher, occupied
herself today packing her few pos
sessions, preparatory to entering
the penitentiary within the next
few days and starting a 20-year
sentence for the murder Of her
father, Trigg Maxwell.


The State Supreme Court Of APP
peals in a brief opinion handed
down yesterday refused her appeal
for a new trial, and the tWo-year
legal battle to save her from prison
ended.

Mrs. Ann Maxwell, mother OF
the teacher, is also under 1ndlct-
ment for the murder and will
probably go on trial within the
next few weeks.


Mrs. Maxwell collapsed when she
heard the high courts refusal to
grant the appeal. Edith took the
decision stoically, saying she had

scribed by Prof William B. Scott and

Notable among these creatures of

gradual reduction of tails, which inter-

County Hospital at Sandy Spring.

AMOY, China, September g.
American residents Of this South
China port of Fukien Province we're
forced to scurry underground today
into bombproof dugouts for protec-
ton against shattering two-hour
raid of Japanese warplanes and war
ships.


American lives we're gravely en-
dangered, and the United States war
ship Asheville was caught in the
bombardment. Several bombs fell only
a short distance from the Asheville
and forced her officers and crew to
hurry below decks for refuge from
the hail of shrapnel.


Oil Plant Endangered.


Bombs and shells from the jap
anese planes and ships rained on
the army headquarters, police head
quarters, the airfield and the old
fort near the compound of the Amer
lean Socony-Vacuum Oil Co.


Two of the bombs crashed near the
Socony plant. Shrapnel showered the
compound, where many of the Amer
ican employees remained at their
posts. Miraculously, the flying chunks
of metal failed to strike either the
personnel or the tanks of inflam.
mable gasoline and oil.


The American colony had previously
prepared bombproof shelters against
such Japanese attack ON this popu-
lou5 city. At the first warning of the
raid they holed-in, safe against the
tWo-hour raid.


Scores of shells were fired from
Japanese cruisers and seven bombs
were counted being dropped by two
seaplanes.


Consulate Is Closed.


From Swatow, 100 miles south of
here in Kwantung Province, the Chi
nese toficiaD Central News Agency
reported two japanese bombers were
shot down and one damaged in a raid
on that port.


United States Ambassador Nelson
johnson today ordered the American
Consulate at Swatow closed and all
Americans evacuated.


His action was taken because of the
increasing danger from Japanese
bombardment Of the important South
China port.


The British steamer Fooshing was
reported to have been halted and
boarded by Japanese blockade patrol
on Annoy yesterday. After a short
delay and examination of her papers
the British vessel was said to have
been allowed to continue her voyage
to Japan.

trawlers

But when the Canarias attacked

NAVALCARNERO. Spain. March

the Madrid front indicated today the
defense high command had moved all
its heavy artillery and most of its
troops to positions along the Valencia
highway, apparently to protect mass
retreat to the Mediterranean Coast.


Although the reports still lacked Of
fetal confirmation, observers declared
the government forces we're building
a strong wall between inSurgent con-
centrations on the Jarama River
front, southeast of Madrid and the
highway connecting the beleaguered
city with the temporary seat OF gov
ernment, Valencia, 100 miles away.


Insurgent headquarters estimated
1000 government soldiers had been
killed on the Jarama River front in
the Insurgent drive which has been
under way there for three weeks. The
estimate OF fatalities was compiled
from figures forwarded to field head
quarters from various sectors.


Insurgent officers asserted that,
even discounting the accounts of cap
tured government militiamen whom
they described as eager to please by
exaggerating government losses, Ma
drid's hospitals were crowded with at
least 1000 wounded

accounts described as evidence the
Madrid defenses were .crumbling.


The slow inroads of Gen. Francisco
Frances troops in nearly four months
of siege were viewed as having driven
defense Commander in Chief Jose
Miaja to consider mass evacuation.

- HE had lpsticked three different mouths


on her own and had decided that the
original Isabelle Cummings lips were
~ still best for her face. She had read the
movie page, the society items" and the
comic strips in the morning paper. She had
talked on the telephone with Kay Oliver for
twenty minutes; she had talked to Susie
Clayton for thirty. She had walked three
times around the front yard.


Now she stood in the back yard, picking
leaves off the syringa bush by the kitchen
steps, Back yards, she thought. were depress-
ing; though her mother certainly saw to it
that this one was neat and green with grass
and kind of like garden. with the three
chairs under the big tree. Nobody hardly ever
sat in the chairs except the cook. On very hot
days Mamie came out and sat down to shell
peas or something.


"Babyw Mamies brown face appeared at
the window above the kitchen sink. "You
want pin t'eat?"


Isabelle shook her head. She strolled over
to the chairs and sat down. A line of poetry
came despairing into her mind:


"Oh, world! oh, life! oh, time'


That was Shelley, she remembered; she had
read It in English class last year. The poem
was all about getting old and dying. She didn't
feel old and dying but she certainly did feel
"Oh, world! oh, life! oh, time!" And oh, what
was the use of it all!


What, indeed - with all the boys in town
having gone off on camping trip the day
before? That is, all the boys who figured in
Isabelle's existence; those young men, just
finished with freshman year in college, who
kept her sixteen year old heart blissful with
their constant attentions.


Two weeks the boys were to be gone. Clos
ing her eyes, Isabelle let her head fall back
against the chair. She certainly wasn't one of
those loathsome females who went around
saying she simply couldn't stand women; she
had as many girl friends as any girl in town.
But after all, two weeks!


She heard the click of the catch on the back
gate and opened her eyes, The delivery boy
from Bailey's Grocery Store was coming up
the walk. striding easily despite the heavy
box on his shoulder and the white apron like
cylinder around his long legs. His shoulders
were wide and his arms tanned and muscular
beneath the rolled-up sleeves of his old shirt.
His hair was yellow, Isabelle saw; and it
glinted in the sunlight. Bailey's must have
changed delivery boys. The last one had
looked like brunette rat.


The boy did not look at Isabelle until he
had carried the box to the kitchen and was
returning down the walk. His glance slid to-
ward her and Isabelle said "Hello!'


Hello" he answered in matter of fact
tone Il didn't think you'd remember me"


You remembered mel" she reminded him.


That's different see you around all the
time" He took dollar watch from his
pocket I'm late. G'by."


"Gby!" her voice, puzzled and questioning,
trailed after him.


In the afternoon when she went riding
around town with Susie Clayton and Kay
Oliver, Isabelle observed abruptly and for
no apparent reason: Delivery boys are GER
tainly peculiar people"


This brought blank stares from the other
two and Isabelle did not, as she had intended,
turn the talk specifically to Bailey's delivery
boy. Obviously. to Kay and Susie, delivery
boyswere creatures from another world. They
wouldn't know who that boy was; or if they
did, they'd think Isabelle had gone crazy
even to want to satisfy her mere curiosity

Epitomizing the reasons why Ger

with gift for epigram said that her
general staff was ready for everything
but the unexpected and prepared for
anything except the inevitable" AS
Hindenburgs chief of staff and quarter
master general, history will give Erich
Ludendorf principal blame for the COM
plex of failures that finally precipitated
the Reichs collapse, but that verdict
will not fail also to accord him credit
for the prodigious and almost successful
resistance which the Kaiser's armies for
four incredible years put up against
literally world of enemies.


Sheer preponderance of brute force,
human and mechanical, that moloch of
military might before which Ludendorff
necessarily burned incense, was doomed
to crush his hopes of victory from the
moment America was able to fling her
illimitable fresh man power into the
crucible of war on the western front.
But until the spring of 1918 triumph
seemed to beckon irresistibly to the
German legions which had successfully
subdued Russia, overwhelmed Italy, oc-
cupied Belgium, Rumania, Serbia and
Eastern France. and, in Sir Douglas
Haig's agonized words, had the British
Army fighting with its back to the wall
To Hindenburg fell the nominal laurels
for the smashing blows which toward the
end seemed to make allied defeat a mere
matter of weeks.


But the real organizer of victory was
the old field marshals younger, more
brilliant subordinate. who from Tannen-
berg on, became the acknowledged tao
tical and strategic genius behind Ger
many's far-flung drive. Unquestionably
Ludendorff will rank among famous gen.
erals of all time, though Nazi eulogies,
which link him with Julius Caesar, Fred
erick the Great and Napoleon, are hyper
bolic. Frank H. Simonds did Ludendorff
full justice when that master American
student of military science wrote: "He
must go down not merely as the man
who lost the war for the Central powers,
but the soldier who came within hairs
breadth of winning it."


Those enviable laurels will enshrine
Ludendorffs name even though his clos
ing years were squandered in pursuit OF
the alterations of neo-paganism, anti
semitism and blind anti-Christian
Wotsn idolatry. Nazidom, worshipping
the same Goddess ideals, appropriately
sounds heros taps over his grave
today.

ERED MCLEOD, the club pro, claims


Columbia will play at least 200
yards longer during the Summer
months when they turn the water on
and the irrigation system gets to work.
Our fairways have gotten pretty hard
during July and August in past years."
says Freddie. up at Chevy Chase
they've found with their watering sys-
tenn that the course plays plenty long
even in the Summer. and we'll have
the same condition here Holes that
the boys have been playing in the
Summer with a drive and a short iron
will become drive and spoon holes be-
cause the tee shots won't run so far.
But they'll have better lies through
those fairways, and the whole course
will be much improved"


Columbia is one of four courses in
this area which have fairway watering.
Chevy Chase pioneered it three years
| ago.


The Five Farms course of the Bal
timore Country Club and the James
River course of the Country Club Of
Virginia use the conveyor sys.enl, by
which water is piped to the fairways
through portable lengths of hose. and
the new nine of the Army-Navy Coun-
try Club is piped for artificial water
ing.

NEW YORK, February 1.-THE


New York Giants. figuratively
speaking, throw out the first ball of
the 1887 base ball season today, when
the first official group, headed by
President Horace Stoneham, sails for
the Havana Spring training camp.
Secretary Eddie Brannick left yester-
day to make arrangements for their
arrival.


Sailing today are Treasurer Leo j.
Bondy and seven players, Jimmy
Ripple and George Davis, outfielders;
Mickey Haslin, inf1elder; Jimmy Shee-
han, rookie catcher, and William
Benne, Tom Ferrick, Cliff Melton
and William Yarewick, all recruit
pitchers.


The rest of the squad, except Man
ager Bill Terry, who is confined to
his home at Memphis by a cold. is
due to assemble at Miami tomorrow
and to reach Havana Friday, a day
ahead Of the New York group. In
Terry's absence Coach Pancho Snyder
will take charge Of training activities.

Western Maryland In II innings yes
terday, one driving in the other with
the winning run.

who also got his early training from
Cliff Moore at Western, found himself
with 20 lead in the sixth but after
hurting five scoreless innings was un-
able to get the side out before three
runs had crossed the plate and Bill
Lanier had relieved him.


In the eighth George Washington
tied the score at A. In the eleventh
Cambell smashed home run for the
Terrors. Winnie de Angels opened the
Colonials' eleventh with a single and
stole second and Edmondson laid down
an intended sacrifice, only to find him.
self on base with the winning run
when Cook, the Terrors' pitcher, fum-
bled the ball.


An infield out set the stage for
Brennan, who poked long single into
center, Edmondson scoring behind
De Angels when Catcher Byrd fun

NANA1MO. British Columbia, June
1.-Two survivors Of the latest acci-
dent in the tragedy-marked history
Of Vancouver Islands mining region
recovered in . hospital here today
while weary rescuers announced two
dead and searched for the body Of
third victim in the flooded Deban coal
mine.


Louis Pognello and John Senini,
Imprisoned in cross-cut 10 hours
after 10000 gallons Of water broke
into the mine from q nearby aban-
doned extension slope, were freed
shortly before midnight.


From their hospital beds they told
how two companions. Nelson Shepherd
and Joe Carr, lost their lives in the
sudden inrush Of water. They said
the fifth man, Joe Shepherd, was
caught In the first flood and prob
ably was carried to the bottom OF the
mine.


Accidents have killed more than
325 persons In the mining district in
the last so years.

Specializing on the hope that
the Adolf Gobel Company's pro-
posed slaughter house at Benning
will not be allowed to operate, the
National Insured Homes Corpora
ton of New York detailed to the
District zoning Commission yester-
day plans for a mililon-dollar hous-
ing development on a 65-acre tract
within 300 yards Of the proposed
abattoir site.


The New York corporation asked
the commission to rezone the
tract to residential area. Portions
Of the tract are now zoned indus
trial and commercial.


Myron Davy, attorney for the
corporation, told the commission
that the tract was purchased last
May by the corporation, which
was fully aware of the slaughter
house question and with the hope
that the Gobel Company will be
denied permission to operate the
abattoir.


Aired D. Calvert, of the Lincoln
Park Citizens Association, which
has gone on record opposing the
abattoir, urged the commission
to defer action until Congress
definitely had settled the slaugh-

Insurgent advices, however, declared
wave after wave of attacking militia
men had been beaten back and the
government forces finally were with
drawing from the dynamite ripped
city.


The insurgent reports admitted,
however, that the garrison had in
trenched itself in underground posi-
tions.


Both besieged and besiegers were
said to be nearly exhausted after
nearly week of fierce fighting. Grimy
fingers firing at triggers and bloodshot
eyes weary at gunsights brought a
comparative lull in the din of battle.


Bilbao dispatches said government
troops had reached Central American
Square and that houses were being
fortified in preparation for fresh
thrlsts to drive the insurgents from
cover.


The Vega Arms Factory, one of the
strongest insurgent positions in the
northwestern Spanish city. fell after
two days of struggle, said Gijon re-
port yesterday.


Capture of the factory was accom-
panied by renewed aerial lombard
ment and dynamite throwing by
''dinamiteros" from the Asturian mine
lands. A squadron of bi-motored
planes swept over the already nearly
ruined city, hurting fresh explosives at
1nsurgent positions.


The "diramiteros," ducking the
spatter Of machine guns, crept close
to houses in the Zabaleda Eguilaz
sector and hurled their sputtering
bundles Of dynamite through the win
dows. The houses burst like toy bal
looms.

Burned by flames Of undetermined
origin while alone in her home late
yesterday. Mrs Anna Kelly, As, of 1411
Thirtieth street NV, died in Gallinger
Hospital early today.


After refusing offers of assistance
from neighbor who heard her
screams. Mrs Kelly lay alone in her
house for three hours before a sister,
Mrs. Mary Buchanan. came home from
work, the latter said


Mrs. Buchanan stated that when
she stepped into the house she noticed
trail Of burned patches in the rugs
leading from the kitchen to an up
stairs bedroom She found her sister
in bed, with nearly all the clothes
burned from her body. The bed. how
ever. showed no evidence of having
been touched by fire


From large patch of ashes on the
kitchen floor, police concluded Mrs.
Kellys dress had in some manner
caught fire in that room and that
after partially extinguishing the flames
by rolling on the floor, she had made
her way upstairs.


Mrs. Buchanan said the neighbor,
Mrs. Alice E. Leiberknight. who lives
in basement of the house, told her
she offered to assist Mrs. Kelly, but
was told her help was not needed.


Mrs. Buchanan said that when she
found her sister she was conscious and
apparently rational, but could not
remember" how the fire started. She
said Mrs. Kelly smoked great deal,
but no cigarette butt was found on
the kitchen floor. Two burned matches
were near wastebasket beside the
gas stove, though the range had not
been lighted, Mrs. Buchanan said.
A former employe of the Bureau of
Engraving and Printing, Mrs. Kelly
retired November because of i'll
health, according to her sister. Mrs.
Buchanan is employed at the Treasury
Department.


Police were investigating the case,
and Coroner A. Magruder Macdonald
announced an autopsy would be held
today.

Like airplanes?" he asked her, his eyes

and she shot in elf-defense

pecked away with stinging left jab

left hooks.

NEW YORK, Dec. 4.-Commodity
prices plunged into new low ground
for the year or longer earlier this week
and then rallied sharply as buying
support entered the market.


At the low point in mid-week. the
Associated Press weighted index of IS
important wholesale spot quotations
was % per cent under the years high
point touched last April.


The index slipped fractionally to
1900 of the 1896 average at the close
OF the period from 76.14 the week be-
fore and compared with 85.43 a year
ago.


Inc excursion into new low territory
that has dominated staple prices in
recent months lost momentum. Foods.
textiles and on-ferrous metals alone
established fresh bottoms for the cur
rent move.


indeed, declines barely outnumbered
advances among commodities included
IN the index. there being l3 dips, IL
increases and 10 unchanged.


Mcct better Demand.


agricultural and industrial items
met good demand when prices scraped
bottom. Both groups were higher on
the week. Underlying the rally, COM
modify men said, was the dearth of
buying in recent weeks with the con-
sequent drop in available supplies.
making replacement orders necessary.
The relatively large setback in live
stock stemmed primarily from the
greater number of animals appearing
on the market. The tight supply DO
sltlon evident earlier this year has
worn off as the summers bumper
crops permitted larger shipments of
fattened animals A minor advance in
hogs was offset by slumps in cattle
and lambs.


Grains moved ahead on receipts of
crop deterioration in other producing
countries; wheat, oats and rye con-
curing. Corn eased slightly.


Cotton Prices Narrow.


Cotton moved narrowly as the trade
attempted to evaluate the effect of
the current harvest-the largest ever
gathered. Although recent world de-
mand for the staple has been good
under existing conditions, analysts
hold, the domestic situation is un-
settled by the trade recession.


Although cotton cloth dipped and
carried with it the index, textile prices
Showed signs of stability as wool and
silk firmed.

fractional decline from the previous
week, according to the McGill Com
modify Service

movement was of fractional nature.


All commodities from the peak this
year have registered decline that
measures Is per cent. Agricultural
products are primarily responsible for
the magnitude of the reaction as this
group is now 25 per cent under the
1887 high.


Meanwhile industrial commodities
have dropped IL per cent and the
third major group-live stock-stands

months ago.

moderate decline during the past
week, rejecting lower prices for hides
and leather, non-ferrous metals, paint
materials, paper and pulp, and tex
tiles.

stokes the furnace with them.

liquidation of grains and metals
pounding quotations steadily down.


Industrial as we'll as farm staples

Every family name has history. But
few such designations trace further back
than the twelfth century. For thousands
of years before that period the average
individual was known solely by given
title. The needs of society barbaric in
character required nothing else than a
tribal classification Only with the be-
ginning of organized industry was there
a demand for distinctively personal
labels


Oliver Wendell Holmes in a poem still
popular speaks of Fate endeavoring to
conceal the author of America by
calling him Smith. Yet originally that
surname was possessed Of a connotation
Of unique importance. During the
Middle Ages the smiths were the me-
chanics, the engineers, upon whom, per-
haps more than upon any other group
Of workers a community depended. They
fabricated the tools used by all their
contemporary craftsmen; they shaped
all materials from gold to iron; they
generally we're prosperous, notably in
telligent civic-minded


Similarly, the Webb and the Weaver
families received their names from the
textile trade in which they were en-
gagged. The Masons, the Millers, the
Coopers, the Tanners, the Taylors, the
Narshalls, the Potters, the Stuarts, the
Clarks, the Cleavers, ETC., represent the
same development. All the Farmers
sprang from agriculturists.


In like manner many citizens adopted
place names from circumstance of resi-
dence. For example, La Fayette sig
nines "a small real estate holding" The

By the Associated Press.


SHANGHAI, August 17.-Prayers of
Thanksgiving were offered on the GUS
toms jetty today before the first DOL
lar Line tender left for the refugee
liner President Jefferson with 1877
American women and children.
1t was strange scene, barren of
JOY even among those fortunate
enough to escape the terrifying bonn
bardments and the threat of hunger
here.


There were no shouts of bon voyage,
no waving handkerchiefs, no steamer
baskets, no flowers, nor were there
any tears and long embraces.
Fathers watching their wives and
children sail to safety stood on the
pier until the tender disappeared down
the river Then they turned, silently
toward the embattled city.
Women Faces Show Strain.
The women, their faces lined by the
strain of long nights of impatient wait
ing amid bursting bombs and anti
aircraft shells, trudged YEARLY aboard.
Most OF them had suit case-their
only luggage-in one hand and child
or two clutching the other One baby
was carried aboard in an incubator.
There was no panic. There we're no
falntlngs. The women and children
had to go, leaving husbands and
fathers behind.


To identify the tender as a neutral
refugee ship officials stretched a big
American flag across an upper deck
like canopy.


1t was the crafts only protection
against the water front aerial, war
ship and artillery duel between the
Chinese and japanese along its peril
Gus 10-mile trip downstream to the
Jefferson's anchorage at Woosung.


Tenders evacuating British refugee
women and children were given q
naval convoy.


Put Safely Aboard.


When the Dollar Line tender re-
turned late today from Woosung,
sailors and United States Marine
Guards who accompanied the refu-
gees brought word they had been put
safely aboard the jefferson


They told of women weeping with
Joy and relief to find themselves safe
aboard the ship, floating island of
refuge from booming guns, with nurs-
cries and food for their children.


Among those who left for Manila
on the President Jefferson were Mrs.
Theodore Roosevelt, jr., and her son
Quentin. Mrs. Roosevelt said she would
return to the United States by the
quickest route possible.


Seamen said the tender ran a CANT
let OF opposing fire, but that both sides
apparently respected its errand of
mercy.


They said the firing was almost
incessant during the whole run down
the 'Vhangpoo River, starting with a
burst of Japanese anti-airclaft fire at
Chinese planes that disappeared in
the clouds few moments after the
tender pulled away from the city.

PEIPING, July II (Sunday) -
Troop trains carrying units of Japan's
powerful Manchurian Army were re-

China trouble zone today as Chinese
and japanese forces resumed their
bitter, intermittent warfare.


They clashed again yesterday and
last night along the Yungting River
about 10 miles west of Peiping, ending
a precarious 36-hour truce. Although
fighting ceased shortly before midnight

break

units of Japan's North China gar

CHICAGO, March 1.-Throughout
the corn belt wagons and trucks
heavily laden with household effects,
live stock and farming equipment
moved in all directions today-March
/, annual moving day for farm
tenants.


Tractors pulling farm machinery
chugged along highways. while the
farm wife, who went to her new
home with the first load, busted her
self arranging furnishings and
Strengthening up. Tomorrow morn
ing school bus drivers will pick up
new charges who wonder if they'll
like their new teachers and class
mates.


Horses and cattle, bit nervous as
they were installed in unfamiliar
barns, neighed and mooed demands
for their customary portions of feed,
corn, oats and hay.


Spring Flowing Near.


The next few weeks will see the
farmer getting everything shipshape-
Spring plowing Is not far away.


1t was not heydey for professional
movers. These tenant farmers, ever
hopeful of accumulating enough to
own their acres, watch their dollars
closely. They use their own equip
ment and swap manpower with their
neighbors.


Upwards of 100000 farm families
changed homes today. a survey of
the Corn Belt States disclosed. Mis-
souri, led with an estimated $4,000
moves. Iowa, where half the 900, 900
farms are tenant operated, counted
probably 16,500 changing tenants.


Advancing prices for farm products,
higher by IA per cent in January than
a year ago. the United States Depart
ment Of Agriculture reports, caused
many tenants to seek larger farms this
year. Others wanted more fertile land.
Still another group moved to farms
they had bought. in many instances
forcing the tenant to vacate.


Shortage Of Farms.


Insurance company farm depart
ment managers and county agents in
Iowa report a shortage of farms this
year. They said some tenants who did
not renew leases before arranging for
other farms have been unable to find
them. Consequently they have been
forced to dispose Of their stock, grain
and equipment and move to town

Life stirred again as it has always done to the
music of spring, for no animate thing can escape
the witchery of that ancient cadence. The
threats of singing birds suddenly became as sill
yer lutes, insects tuned their fairy fddles,
while in the swamps the musty silence was
crashed by the cultural diapason of bullfrogs.


Even old Itswoot, the she-grizzly that ruled
the hills of the Ohanepecosh, felt the intoxica
ton of the moment as she broke through the
shell-ice at the mouth of her winter cave and
drank deeply of the morning wind from the
south.


Although terrifying figure ordinarily, by
reason of her vast bulk and evident power, at
thisinstant she seemed almost gentle and kindly,
as though aware that she had been blessed by
Fate, for beside her was tiny cub, eyes bright
and big ears perked in comical fashion as he
gazed upon strange world whose immensity
and vastness made him tremble in awe. The
warmth of her great mother love had softened a
nature made hard by the unrelenting warfare
of man.


Old ST Phann and other hillmen of the Ohane
pecosh had often puzzled over the fact that they
had never seen Itswoot with cub trailing her.
She was wary, and on the rare occasions that
they had glimpsed her, she had been alone. Re-
peatedly they tried to kill her because hard
pressed by hunger, she sometimes raided the
sheep flocks that grazed the highlands in
summer.


Because she was always alone, they finally
concluded that she was barren, and they re-
joioed Eventually she would die, and focks and
herders would no longer be troubled by the
presence of grizzly in those rugged hills They
would have been astonished to learn that four
times Itswoot had mothered cub.


Three times chance had decreed that she
should NOPE and grieve for days over the un
expected death of soft ft-furred baby, upon
whom she lavished all her affections. But now
the miracle of motherhood had recurred once
more, and surely this little cub. more beautiful
in her eyes than the others had been. would
live and thrive and come into his heritage as
monarch of the high country.


The first of the youngsters had died in the
cave of its birth when Itswoot accidentally
rolled upon it. For long hours she had sorrowed
alone while trying to coax life back into the
pitifuy small form by tenderly licking it. This
failing, she had quilted the cave ahead of time,
while snow still lay deep on the ground. and
had never gone back, even when Billiards
scourged the land

slide soon after she led it out into the world and
she had not seen it again. although she searched

homeland, declared today that "our
territory has been conquered. but not
the spirit of the Basque people"


ut is never conquered" the defeated

striking their objective with several

The Internal Revenue Bureau ruled

empt from corporation taxes.


This exemption applies, the bureau
said, even though employe beneficiaries
may be required to make regular con-
tributions to the mutual benefit fund,
and even if contributions also are made
by employers.


In another ruling, the bureau held
that persons engaged in producing
maple sirup are not agricultural
laborers, and therefore are subject to
social security taxes.


A third ruling said that payments
from union to a member for time
lost from his regular employment while
serving as a negotiator for the union
constitute wages and are taxable under
the security law.

PEIPING, August 28.-Japanese
military authorities today claimed
complete occupation of strategic Man.
kow Pass, the 12-mile-long gateway
to Inner Mongolia. after bloody 16-
day battle in which Chinese troops
contested every inch of the way.


Trustworthy sources said that the
victory had cost about $500 Japanese
lives.


japanese Follow Railroad.


The victorious japanese forces now
are f1anking westward along short
section of the Pingsui Railroad. which
the Chinese still hold above the pass.
japanese forces, which previously
claimed capture of Kalgan, the Chinese
military base north of Peiping, now are
deploying eastward from Hsuanhua,
flanking the north side of the railway
and sandwiching 10000 Chinese troops
between 40-mile fronts.


A wide gap in the Japanese lines
still would permit the easy fight of
the Chinese to the southwest toward
Tatung in Shansi Province, it was
said.


japanese domination of the steep
walled gateway to Inner Mongolia
was believed to have been offset by
the dynamiting of railway tunnels by
the retreating Chinese, making them
useless for railway traffic.


Great Wall Breach Reported.


Previously it had been reported that
part of Japan's North China Army
Of 10000 men had broken through
The Great Wall and were closing in
vlselike on the stubborn defenders
Of NankoW Pass


Japanese battalionS were said to
have skirted Chinese positions, clam
berlng over precipitous Lodges and
into the valley behind the Chinese
A whole japanese regiment was sew
cred from the main force and its base
of supplies before it succeeded in
turning the Chinese flank on 4,200-
foot ledge commanding the pass.


In this North China conflict the
Japanese are outnumbered nearly
two to one. The Chinese strength has
been estimated at 225,000.

BETHESDA. Md, March 25.-While
recovering from gas explosion in
her home Monday, Mrs. Rebecca Anna
Rea, 36, wife of Courts D. Rea.
Social Security Board official, was
fatally injured early today when she
jumped from her attic window, ac-
cording to police reports.


DR.. Benjamin c. Perry, who had
been treating Mrs. Rea since she
was critically injured by the explosion
of the kitchen stove, told police that
she had leaped from a small window
above the bed room of her home at
45l5 Ridge avenue, Chevy Chase, and
evidently suffered fractured skull
She was dead upon arrival at the
Georgetown Hospital where she was
taken by the Bethesda fire depart
ment rescue squad.


Officer William Crawford of the
Montgomery County Police said that
Mrs. John Turner, sister of Mrs. Rea,
who lives at 815 Eighteenth street in
Washington, spent the night at the
Rea home. She reported that neither
had slept during the night and that
about 445 am. Mrs. Rea got out Of
bed and paced the floor. She said she
offered her sister a sedative but it
was refused. Mrs. Turner then drop
ped off to sleep and when she awak-
ened half an hour later, she told po-
lice, her sister was no longer In the
room.


She called her brother-in-la who
was sleeping in room across the hall,
and when they noticed that the trap
door at the top of the ladder leading
to the attic was open Rea went to the
hall window and saw his wife lying in
the driveway. Her body fell about 35
feet She apparently landed on the
back Of her head


Rea summoned Dr.. Perry, who noti-
fed police.


Mrs Rea was rescued from the
kitchen of her home Monday, after
Mrs. Richard Cunningham. who lives
across the street, at 4512 Ridge street,
saw flames in the rear of the house
and notified police. The explosion had
blown the door between the kitchen
and dining room off its hinges, broken
several windows and blown one of
the kitchen window frames into the
yard next door.


Mrs. Rea was found lying on three
chairs in front of the oven door of
the kitchen stove, and a note, the
contents of which Montgomery County
police refused to reveal, was found
Inv Goyeyo1 Of tho
open. Police explained that the gas
probably was ignited by the stove s
pilot light.

NEW YORK, September 20-The
continuing uptrend in individual pur-
chasing power should prove adequate
to maintain wearing apparel sales at
profitable levels and to absorb rising
labor and material costs over the next
several months, according to Poor's
Industry and Investment Surveys.


With individual consumer income
still moving upward, the average Gus
toner Is becoming less price con-
scious, and once more favors better
quality apparel.


Rising labor and material costs are
inevitably forcing price mark-ups in
most lines of clothing and accessories"
states the analysis. Consequently
the problem Of gradual consumer re-
sistance to higher prices tends to
cloud the more distant business hor-
izon for both manufacturing and mer-
chandising divisions of the apparel
industry. In general, however, indi-
cations point 10 full year 1887 profits
somewhat above the 1896 levels. 1t
seems likely, moreover, that propor-
tionately greater gains may be ex-
pected for those companies specializing
IN quality products and catering to
consumers in the higher income
brackets.


Those manufacturers of mems
shirts and underwear who maintain
their quality regulations will benefit
most from currently expanding sales.
The silk hosiery division faces long
term declining trend owing to the in
creasing competition from rayon and
from mercerized materials, but this
has been temporarily offset as a result
OF rising consumer purchasing power.
Companies engaged in the processing
OF fur are particularly well situated
to reap the benefit of luxury demand
and sre enjoying continued improve
ment"

birds which nest seven months every

Juan Capistrano Mission take off for
South America October %, San Juans
day.

today only a. few laggards fluttered
about for the hundreds of tourists who

the flock began to thin two weeks ago.


The thousands of swallows usually
leave at dawn during their stay here to
forage for insects. They return at SUM-
set and so are seldom seen even at the
height Of their season.

ing mammothS.

cinity. drowning one crew member

Senators and representatives
from agricultural States were set
today to block the bills now before
Senate and House to provide a
five-day work week for Federal
employees.


Senator Bulow CD of South
Dakota, chairman of the Senate
Civil Service Committee, is one.
The Logan bill for five-day week
is before his committee. The
South Dakota Senator, whose
State is predominantly agricul-
tural, admitted that he was not
enthusiastic over the proposal.
FEAR CONSTITUENTS


Even members from industrial
districts said privately it would
be difficult for them to vote for
five-days-work week for Federal
employees while their own con.
stituents are working six days.


It is being recalled that mem
bers Of Congress from the farm
ing States voted almost unani-
mously for the economy act Of
1888, freezing" the Federal pay
roll by suspending promotions and
containing the controversial mar.
Mcpherson clause (Section 213),
prohibiting the employment Of
husband and wife by the Federal
Government. This clause was only
recently repealed.


BLOCKS TIME BILL


Farm Senators and Congress
men have also been responsible
for blocking daylight-saving legis-
lation, desired by city workers and
labor groups.


Analysis of the Senate Civil
Service committee shows that all
Of it's members-Democrats and
Republicans alike-come without
exception from agricultural States.


On the House Committee, there
are a few urban legislators, but
for the most part members repre-
sent agricultural districts.

LA PLATA, Argentina, February a.
Baby Eugenio Peyrera Iraola, Argen-
tina's ''Lindbergh baby" was found
today, the life choked out of his little
body, five years almost TO the day
after Charles A. Lndbergh, jr, was
kidnapped from Jerseys Sourland Hills.
Like Baby Lindbergh, 2-year-old
Eugendo, the seventh child Of baronial
cattle wealth, was killed by his kid
naper. He was stripped Of his little
suit, choked and wounded, and left,
his arms crossed on his chest, in the
slime Of pigpen at the edge Of beau
tiful La Sorpresa. his parents estate.


Five years ago next Monday the
Lindbergh baby was kidnapped from
his famous parents Hopewell, N. j.,
estate. precipitating perhaps the most
intense man hunt in American annals.
1t led to finding of the child's broken
body two months later, not far from
his secluded home.


Bruno Richard Hauptmann paid for
the crime in Jerseys electric chair.
Murder Hunt On.


Argentina's greatest murder hunt
was on tonight Several suspects a.
ready were held. But police were re-
luctant to decide whether one of these
was the bearded man" who carried
little Eugenio away last Wednesday
evening. and presumably strangled
MIN before he was left in the pigpen,
mile and half from his rambling,
luxurious home.


Police, armed with rifles, averted
what might have been lnching at
tempt when a menacing crowd, with
ire mounting against hobo suspect,
Jose Gancedo, gathered around the
Mar Del Plata jail after news spread
that Eugenio's body had been found


A strong guard was thrown around
the jail, but the crowd remained in
the vicinity throughout the afternoon.


A police communique tonight an
nounced the baby's death was due to
Strangulation. There were no other
marks of violence except scratches,
probably caused by wire through which
the kidnaper dragged the child be-
| tween the house and the scene of the
killing.


Police said Eugenio's clothing was
| found in perfect condition" in
cornfield about half a mile from the
spot where the body was discovered.
! 1t was believed the blue-eyed child
had been slain Thursday, the day after
he disappeared. On that day and the
day afterward provincial and federal
officers spread vast dragnet over the
fashionable Mar del Plata resort
countryside near the great Estancia.
Volunteer searchers, hunting side by
| side with bronzed workers, combed
fields and pampas for clues.
First word today that Eugenio had
been found sent his grandfather, the
powerful Senator Antonio Santa Ma
rina. racing from Mar del Plata for
the Estancia in a motor car with phy-
sicians on the hope the baby was still
alive


| It was lost hope.


! The childs father. Simon Peyrera
Iraola, wealthy horse breeder who
had been directing the search from
Mar del Plata, also rushed to La Sor-
presa, but the baby's mother remained
in the resort city, stricken with grief.


In jail at Mar del Plata was wan.
dering peon, Jose Gancedo, whose
mumbled monosyllables gave no an
swer to why he disappeared from the
Estancia Wednesday night.


Mar del Plata police also held Jose
and Daniel Silva, jose's wife Teresa
| -
a short time ago been discharged as
administrator of the 6,600-acre estate
of the Peyrera Iraola family.


Gancedo had recently shaved on
his beard. but police declined to say
whether they thought he was the
mysterious bearded stranger whom
Eugenios 5-year-old brother Miguel
saw pick up the baby Wednes lay eve
ming in the Estancia garden.
! Under Physicians Care.
| Little Miguel N.nself was placed
under doctors care.


Newspaper reports said the babys
wealthy grandfather had indicated a
willingness to pay ransom. and that
he had been in contact with the kid
naper, but authorities declined to con-
firm the report.


The remnants Of the dead bandit
Baby Face" Gordillos gang were
suspected by police at beginning of
the search, but later authorities in
dicated a moral outcast was sought.


Dull-faced Gancedo-the "linyera,"
or hobo. who police said was the
principal suspect-viewed the pitiful
body of little Eugenio in the COM
pany of investigators, but showed no
sign of emotion.


While a medical investigation was
under way to determine if the boy
died directly from Strangulation, as
the marks on his throat indicated,
police took Gancedo to view the body
and the scene where Eugenio was
found dead.


Authorities said that Gancedo was
subnormal mentally.

into custody when found hiding under

text:
CAIRO, April ia travelogue
combining the thrill of the seldom
visited Egyptian oasis, with the sup
plement of a strange voyage up the
White Nile, is now offered the tourist
who visits Egypt.


Today old Khartoum remains a his
toric memory closeted with the relics
OF Stanley's stirring march and Lord
kitchener's reconquest in the city's
magnificent museum of antiquity,
which is surrounded by the finest ZOO
logical gardens in the world. Strangely
contrasted with this modernity, near
the city are the sacred balloon-shaped
hut encampments and holy Shrines of
African devotees. Three miles from
the modern city stands the century,
old mud brick community of Omdur-
man, the African metropolis of 25 900
native dervishes, who, in flowing white
robes, turbaned sheik headgear, now
welcome the tourist.


Thirty Miles of Bazaars.


AS the steamer heads toward Kawa
the shoreline is ended by innumerable
shore-bank markets, where the brown
races exhibit their wares of ornamen-
tai carved tusks, bright red and yellow
slippers with the upturn pointed toes
of fashion, neckwear, swords and cur
ious f1ligree designs which attract the
nomads of the surrounding desert. The
vast corridor of bazaars stretches as
an emporium for 80 miles. Beyond the
trading centers the traveller glimpses
the first native villages of the Suks,
who hold the Niles distinction for
gaudy costume.


AS the steamer nears Renk, 290
miles from Khartoum, the modern
world slips away and history repeats
itself. Here on the banks live the
Shilluks in grass-thatched villages. A
few miles beyond begins the land of
the Dinkas. where half-naked ebony
giants practice their weird barbaric
customs and one may see their exhi-
billions of shore forest of glittering
spears in the daily war maneuvers of
Africa's tribesmen.


Hippos, Savages and Civilization.


This region also introduces the
huge horned heads of buffaloe, viewed
above the elephant grass, and the
hippo who rises above the shining
surface of the water and seeks shore
on the approach of the steamer. From
this point the passenger has the
strange experience of living in an
other world, for the steamer becomes
an oasis of civilization, gliding down
sea framed by arbarism. The
unique costumes, the feathered head
gear, millions of beads, bracelets that
decorate dark skins, all add to the
memory book Of the exciting and
exotic experience.


No less strange and fascinating are
the journeys to the oasis. The visitor
who conceives these places as a little
grass and sparse water is surprised to
find a fertile country with houses and
walled gardens, growing pomegranate,
orange, lemon, mish-mish, mulberry

MEMPHIS, Tenn, February 13-
A yellow floodtide that despoiled
cities, towns and farms in the valleys
OF the Ohio and Mississippi coursed
toward the Gulf today while an alert
legion of workers manned the lower
valley levees.


The billion-dollar levee line held
firm and Army engineers and veterans
of many high-water fights foresaw
victory over the greatest food in the
Nations history.


Stricken cities along the Ohio began
to dig from under the slime Of
devastation, strewn with the wreckage
of countless homes and buildings.
The death list stood at 466.


Ohio Falls Rapidly.


The Ohio fell rapidly along its en-
tire course below Cincinnati. The
Mississippi's retreat quickened from
Cairo, ILL.,, to Helena, Ark, where
levee defenders watched the passing
crest leave bulwarked dikes intact.


With the passage of the big rivers
peaks, the choked tributary streams
in Southeast Missouri, East Arkansas
and West Tennessee will begin drain
ing, releasing hundreds of thousands
of acres and numerous small towns
inundated by muddy backwaters.


The principal worry of levee patrols
was the menace Of sandboils that
bubbled up behind the earthen bar
riers from the tremendous pressure of
the flood. One burst out in a New
Orleans riverside street yesterday, but
was quickly controlled with a ring Of
sandbags.


Lake Is Safety Valve.


Additional needle gates were pulled
in the Bonnet Carre Spillway, 80 miles
above New Orleans, to divert greater
burden of the water into Lake Pont-
chartrain, safety valve used for the
first time.


The river dropped beneath SIS feet
at Cairo, more than feet below the
crest. The rate of recession increased
at New Madrid, Mo; Hickman, KY,
and Memphis.


The Red Cross, guardian of nearly
100000 homeless. prepared to return
refugees to their homes wherever
possible.

last night Of Mrs. Lula Corvin. 81. d.

Commonwealths Attorney J. L. Dill
low, who investigated the killing, said
today that Fillinger shot the two wom-
en- as they lay in bed together at

roomed at the Corvin home, emptied
.38 caliber revolver at the women
several bullets striking Mrs. Corvin

machine

The panic stricken exodus of Chi

SHANGHAI, Nov 18-Japanese
Army spokesmen announced tonight
that Japanese troops driving to break
through China's "Hindenburg" line
between Shanghai and Marking had
captured one gate of the walled city
of Kashing, southern keystone of the
line.


Both Chinese and japanese reported
heavy fighting in the area around
Kashing, so miles southwest of Shang-
hal and 30 miles south of Soochow,
main point of Chinese defenses.


Chinese told of spirited engage
ment at Seven Star Bridge, 4 miles
northeast of Kashing. japanese said
they were unable to state officially
that their forces had captured the
city.


Civilians Flight Spurred.


News of the japanese push against
the southern wing of the defenses
stretching from the Yangtze River
south to Hangchow Bay came a few
hours after an unoficial government
warning spurred mass migration Of
civilians from Marking.


For "a hours Chinese had held their
own along the length of the defenses
to which they retreated after Shang-
hal fell into japanese hands Novem-
ber 9.


Although the Japanese received re-
Inducements for the new onslaught
today, their only advance apparently
was on the southern front. They
were unable to push forward toward
Soochow. along the Shanghai Marking
Railroad.
