by 20 warplanes, had counter attacked
and pushed japanese back toward
Cheni They also asserted Chinese
had repulsed three Japanese attempts
to effect a landing at Fushan, 100
miles downstream from Nanking on
the Yangtze.


Creeks, Canals Aid Defense.


The japanese explained that Chinese
lines from Soochow north to the
Yangtze were protected by a network
OF creeks and canals and defended
by 100000 troops under the command
OF Gen. Pal Chung-hsi, leader of
Kwangsi Province forces and once
a bitter foe Of Generalissimo Chang
kal-shek.

BARCELONA, May 29.-Govern-
ment authorities said today they had
frustrated an insurgent plot to seize
the Island Of Minorca with the aid OF
5000 troops from neighboring NAL
lorca, allegedly the base for insurgent
aerial attacks on Spains eastern coast


The coastal City of Valencia, tenn
porary capital of the Spanish govern
ment, meanwhile counted 200 dead
after yesterdays dawn air raid that
laid waste to sections OF the crowed
city and spread terror among the in
habitants.


The plot to add Minorca to the in
surgent territory was aided by band
OF l3 Minorcan Fascists, government
authorities said. The leader was re-
ported to have committed suicide
when the others were arrested.
They were said to have prepared to
aid the landing of Italian troops from
Mallorca.


Ninety Bombs Released.


In the Valencia raid more than 90
bombs were rained from the attacking
planes, which observers said were of
Italian manufacture.


The merchant ship Cabin, flying the
British flag, was struck in Valencia
Harbor and six members of the crew
were killed and eight injured The
British freighter Pinzon also was
struck, but the projectile failed to ex-
plode.


The British Embassy declared the
Pinzon was the only British ship"
damaged, lending mystery to the reg
istry of the Cabin.


More than so buildings were dam
aged in the raid, including a plainly
marked Red Cross Hospital.


Raid Called "Diabolical."


Among the American witnesses of
the Valencia attack was Socialist
Norman Thomas. who described the
raid as "diabolical" He said he would
make flrst-hand report to President
Roosevelt and urge him to take a
firmer stand against the Italo-G German
war against Spanish women and
children"


Thomas, with his wife and other
Americans, was visiting in the tenn
porary Spanish capital.

waters

consul. L. Kurz, German consul at

passed line and attempted to get

result. Capt. Liebert directed the

relocating was halted, he went to his
cabin.

wounded. When Coast Guard officers
arrived he was dead.

Argument in the textile confer

ternational labor office in Geneva,

MADRID, Dec. 31.-More than 2O0,-

and 200 airplanes today were thrown
into the greatest battle of the civil
war. outside Teruel.


The bitterness of the fight developed
from a powerful insurgent counter
offensive to take that city, into which
the government fought its way last
week.


More tanks, airplanes, artillery and
men than in any previous single battle
were thrown together in the conflict
which began on Wednesday.


Government lines on the right and
center of the front we're reported
holding under terrific pressure. The
government gave ground on the left.
however. losing some positions which
were considered here to be unim-
portant.


Thirty insurgent tanks participated
IN one engagement along the railroad
line yesterday. Government observers
counted more than 100 insurgent air.
planes IN the air at one time.


B0mbers Protected.


About $50 insurgent pursuit planes
We're sent up to protect 40 bombers
harassing government positions north
and west of Teruel and the CITY itself


IhlS powerful concentration of air.
craft. described as the greatest mass
ing OF planes in the war, outstripped
air activity on the Guadalaja lara front
last February when 12O warplanes
were used.


Scores Of heavy artillery pieces also
were employed by the insurgents as
their forces advanced toward Concud
across open terrain and from Fezas
toward Campillo. Intense hand-to-
hand fighting developed in many
places.


Government commanders estimated
twice as many men were engaged as
were ever used before in single civil
war battle. They said the insurgents
brought shock troops from other
fronts along with practically all equip
ment used in the Asturias campaign.





Few Prisoners Taken.

occupied the Bank Of Spain Building
in Teruel yesterday after mining it.
They took few prisoners, the report
said. as majority of the defenders
were killed in the fighting and the
explosion. A short-wave radio trans
mitter was found.


Latest advices said government
troops captured the whole front part
OF block Of houses overlooking Plaza
San Juan. The insurgents still we're
holding various civil buildings and a
hospital.


Government troops broke into the

defenders were reported to have re-

June IS (P).-Grim Basque militiamen

| started their drive against BASQUE

reported to have been the last English
man in Bilbao His staff and other
British nationals were evacuated long
ago.

By the Associated Press.


HENDAYE, Franco-Spanish Border,
June l8-Two divisions of Basque
defenders fell back to their rear
guard positions west of Bilbao today
to keep open the road for retreat to
Santander as the government fled the
never conquered northern capital.


Meanwhile, in the eastern suburbs OF
the city of Mount Archanda. the leg
weary rebel troops came within sight
of Loyalist snipers and the fires in the
city. They awaited only the compile
tion of an encircling movement by
troops toiling up the torturous hills to
the west of Bilbao before making the
push to enter Bilbaos limits.


But frightened refugees brought out
stories of Basque capital fortified
with cobblestone barricades and hid
den mines for fight to the finish.


All bridges that led into the new
city" across the Nervion River are
mined, the refugees said. The main
streets are crisscrossed with the cob
blestone barricades.


Insurgents declared they held COM
plete control Of the eastern reaches
of the Nervion River, Bilbao's avenue
to the Bay Of Biscay, and were launch
ing the long-awaited pinching move
ment to drive the Basques from the
western hills and incloSe the city.


The official Basque delegation at
Bayonne, France, announced the gov
ernment of the semi-autonomous re-
public had left its besieged capital
"for another point in Basque terri
tory"


The location of the new capital
was being kept secret fo- military
reasons, but one report said the gov
ernment had taken up its seat at the
little village of Trucios, about 20 miles
west Of Bilbao, on secondary road
to Santander.


Defense Command Named.


Before they left they turned over
the military command to a new de-
fense junta composed of Gen. Gamir
Uribarri, chief defense commander;
Jesus Leizaola, minister of justice;
Santiago Aznar, minister of industry,
and Juan de Astigarrabia, minister
of public works.


While Basque shock troops slowed
up the enemy advance to protect the
retreat of their main body and the
withdrawal of artillery batteries and
stores of ammunition, the third and
fourth Basque divisions reached the
rear-guard positions and occupied
them.


The Basques were apparently mass
ing all their forces west of the city
to prevent Generalissimo Francisco
Frances insurgents from capturing
the dominant heights, cutting the
highway to Santander and bottling
up the capital. Bilbao, incidentally,
is withstanding its fifth siege in 100
years.


Population Swollen.


The shelling of the city from the
insurgent gun implacements on the
eastern outskirts continued through
out the night, the defense junta de-
clared, with pursuit planes flying only
200 feet above the streets, machine
cunning everything in range


"One hundred fifty thousand per-
sons have been evacuated from Bill
bao to Santander by land and sea

These make up the fascinating COL
lection of Bevan Allen, 6, OF 3ll4 Dunn

years, has been building up an exhibit
through which he's learning much
about sea life.


Some Of his items have been gifts
from friends, such as the strange
specimens an aunt sent from Florida.
Others Bevan collected on vacation
trip to Bethany Beach, Del, where he
first became interested in this absorb
ing hobby.


But the shell Bevan prefers to all
others come, oddly enough, not from
beach, but from high cliff overlook
ing Yorktown, Va. And. after finding
it, Bevan learned little geology he'd
never known before.


II couldn't imagine how 1t got
there" he declared in exhibiting the
large black shell he'd brought home
with him. But 1 found lots of them,
and they are all thousands and thou
sands of years old"


Bevan is quite right.


His shell is that old, in all likelihoodf
much older.


Long ago the land where Yorktown
now stands was covered by the sea.
Shells were deposited along its shore.


Gradually the shore, with its shells,
sank under water. Mud and sand col
lected on top of the shells. Long after
that the land was raised from out the
water. Streams and rivers cut their
way through it and once more the
shells were exposed to the sunshine.
Now they may be gathered from that
old. old beach which has become part
of the cliffs overlooking Yorktown.


But this bit of information Is not
the only history Bevan remembers
when he looks at his shells.


1t was at Yorktown, you recall. that
the last great battle of the Revolution
was IOuRnt III tol. llClC tiiC hiiSA
ican Army and the French Fleet sur
rounded the British. Some of the
French battleships were sunk during
the seige, but recently they have been
raised from the bottom of the York
River.


All through the vessels are found
boat worms, living by eating the water
soaked timbers of the old ships. These
fishlike worms that feast on any wood
en- ship under the. water line live in
little tubular shells. And Bevan, alert
collector that he is. has several shell
tubes which he gathered in and near
the old French vessels.


With such interesting background
connected with his shells, Bevan has
found his collection welcome exhibit
in his school assembly.


And visitors at his home are often
entertained with view of his box of
shells as he is delighted to share his
hobby with folks who are interested.

Saturday. Total points for all heats
determined the winners.


Naturally, the time in all classes

~ ORT WASHINGTON, N. Y,
- September 2O.-Although the
Pimm, Germany's entry in the


fifteenth annual star class
yacht world championship, has won
three straight races and stands a good
chance to make it four by winning
the fifth and final race of the series
today, the title may 60 to an Amer
ican boat that has placed second,
fifth and sixth twice in four trials.


A thin wire that broke was all that
prevented the international title from
going to European boat for the first
time since the world championships
began. The wire, jib shroud. broke
aboard the Pimm during the first
race, throwing the rigging out of bal
ance and bending the mast. The
Pimm came across the line In twenty
second position, but won the next
three races. Yesterday the Pimm came
in more than quarter OF mile ahead.


Lecky Needs Only Fifth Place.
EVEN though the Pimm finishes first


again today, the Lecky, skippered
by Milton Wegeforth OF San Diego
Calf, has only to repeat yesterdays
performance to take the championship
The Lecky, second the first day and
sixth in the next two races, finished
fifth yesterday to total 129 points,
six more than the Pimm's total Fifth
or better today gives the Lecky the
title.


Should the Lecky finish sixth, while
the Pimm takes first place, the point
total would be tied, but the German
boat would win the title because it
has beaten the Lecky more times than
the Lecky has defeated the Pimm.

Thirty Americans Narrowly
escaped death in the first raid on
Canton. Refugees from the Yang
tie Valley, they had just left the
Canton Hankow railroad station
when Is Japanese planes began
aiming missiles at the building


At least 80 persons were killed

combatants living in the slums
the station. Six were killed in the
station itself.


While scores Of anti-aircraft
guns popped away, Chinese sol
diers with fixed bayonets drew up

prevented any accurate check on

Twelve airplanes roared over
the capital twice and bombed the
Pukow railroad station a few miles
outside the town. Chinese war
ships anchored down the Yangtze
River also were attacked.


In the face Of those daily raids
on Marking. the populace is re

in the vacuum created when short sup
plies met heavy demand commodity
prices chalked up the eighth con-
secutive weekly advance in the latest
period to the highest point since late
1929.


Spot inventories of many staples
have declined steadily for months.

those items dominated by foreign pro-
ducers working under restriction
agreements such as rubber. copper, tin
! and the like

creases. created a sellers market.

Live stock, industrial and agricu1-

ferrous metals were also higher Tex

tional performance, pushing ahead
sharply as exporting countries dis

on reports of continued dryness in the

abroad. Corn. oats, rye and cotton
shared the upturn.

marked up, turpentine yielded a frac-

She glanced down at him. His breathing was
almost normal and his face had lost the heated
flush of fever. The room seemed cooler, too.
She wondered whether she imagined that the
air had grown less heavy and oppressive; she
felt almost chilly, but she was sure that it
must be due to fatigue and strain.


For two nights and two days, she had
scarcely moved from the bedside. The young
doctor had said, IF we can break the fever,
Mrs. Dawson, we'll pull your husband out of
this and have him on his feet in no time. He
was new in the community, and took for
granted that Harriet was Jims wife, Mile,
lowering fearfully in the background, had
made no attempt to disillusion him. She pre-
ferred to remain downstairs and did her
meager best at fighting the dust and prepar-
ing the meals.


The long hours had been punCtuated by
John Dawson standing at the door with trays
of unpalatable food which made Harriet long
to cut herself in two so that she need not
leave him to Miles inadequate ministra-
TONS Her heart ached for him. He had been
able to face everything but Jim's illness. He
would come into the room and mutely look
down at the bed, and walk out again, too
shaken to speak. Harriet had tried to pour
hope into him, but there were times when she
too knew only despair. Drought. heat, dust.
To what end? And why?

INA few minutes the train would bring Jim


Dawson back from college; to the wheat


lands he loved, to the farmer-father who


needed him, and to Harriet. whose heart
was bursting with happiness. Harriet had
been raised with Jim as his adopted sister, but
since he d been away she'd grown into wom-
an, the prettiest girl in the county," said
Inns father, who knew her worth and shared
her secret hopes.


Harriet was so ecstatic when Jim stepped
off the train that at first she did not notice
Mile When jim turned and proudly brought
forward the girl with the red hat and crisp
yellow curls - my wife, we were married
yesterday" - Harriet tried to speak, but her
whole body felt numb with the sudden shock.


1t took only few hours to reveal Mile as
cheap and shallow thing whom Jim had met
in dance hall, and who had fallen in love"
with him when she heard that his father
owned eight hundred acres Less than an hour
on the farm. August-hot and beginning to feel
the pinch of drought, made her shrily deter
mined to get Jim away to the city. She hated

also guessed the hopeless, hitherto unsus-
pected love of Joseph, the hired man. for
Harriet, and made tawdry jokes about it.
Before the first night in her new home Mile
had churned its placid life into a storm of
hate and jealousy and fear.


Harriet realized that she was now an in
truder in the house which had been home.
She packed her bags to 60 she knew not
where, but before she could leave, the dust
storm broke on the farm in choking fury. The
well went dry, some of the cattle had to be
shot, Jim became delirious with dust pneu-
monia Mile, frightened, put through secret
call to an old flame in Kansas City, planning
to escape Harriet, fearful for what disillusion-
ment would do to Jim, restrained her from
leaving.


But Millie would not answer the insistent
calls for her from the sick room. What should
Harriet do? After moments indecision she
went up to Jim, put her arms around him.
I'm here, darling" she whispered. Miles
with YOU Go to sleep, darling" He sighed
and closed his eyes, and she held him close
against her breast.

text:
Mother Nature was rough in the
making of New England. The
Jagged northern coastline evi-
denceS ancient upheavals and the
sandy southern shores show
where glaciers finally stopped their
pulverizing and melted back into
the north.


Before the ice the numerous
mountain ranges were piled up by
titanic stresses in the earth's sur
face and then when the ice came,
miles thick, they were secured off
and rounded, the valleys channeled
deeper and the boulders StreWn
far and wide.


But there was plenty of time
before man came on the scene to
make of all this the finest recrea-
tional resources. The mountains,
except for few bolder peaks, be-
came verdant; springs grew into
streams and rivers, the action of
the sea began to work on the coast
line.


Mountains Always Near


New England has been be-
Queathed wonderfully various
terrain. Man has changed it but
little, and then only to make it
more readily accessible and useful.
You have read about the sea and
its part in New England life. Now
consider its mountains.


Somewhere in almost every New
England scene there is a mountain.
At Lafayette National Park in
Maine a pink granite motor road
winds to the top of Cadillac Noun
tain, where you may gaze over the
rounded hills and far out over the
Atlantic.


Hiker's trails, marked with log
cabins and other shelters for the
night, open up vast regions where
the automobile cannot penetrate.
Connecticut has it's Litchfield
Hills, broken and secretive, with
winding rivers down in deep-cut
valleys.


The Litchfield Hills are indivi-
dual masses, with frequent small
and cupshaped valleys between
them, or they are little plateaus.
The old roads which threaded
through and over them had to
wind and twist, getting up from
the river gorges, or leading from
one town to the next. Old villages
once isolated charm the traveller
along his way.


BerkshireS Different


The Berkshires, in Massachus-
etts, connect with the Litchfields,
yet they are quite different. They
lie mostly in long horizontals with
both wider and longer valleys be-
tween, giving wholly different
landscape effect. Here is the
scene of stirring colonial history,
of warfare with the Indians and
then with the English. Later the
fine old towns attracted such
figures as Nathaniel Hawthorne,
Henry Ward Beecher, Herman
Melville and Oliver Wendell
Holmes. Nowadays great resorts
and handsome summer homes dis
tinguish the region.


Moving on up to Vermont one
enters the Green Mountains, a
long, majestic backbone" of the
State. All through them are
scattered broad and smiling lakes.

srously applauded, the Coolidge Quar-

two standard compositions BY Beetho-
ven and Haydn.


FOR the &C Minor Quartet, Op. 10.
No. t." by Beethoven, written in light
vein, the players adopted . pleasing
mexyo-voice quality Of tone suited to
the type Of the composition. Singing
passages interviewer with . playful
mood here and there. made one forget
the more serious Beethoven. The vol
ume Of tone used, while charming In
its effect, was tinged with too much
intention to be perfectly satisfying.
No marked difference in style Of treat
ment was made between this number
and Haydn's "Divertimento in E Flat,
attributed to Haydn's youthful period.
which was second on the program.
Many graceful Embellishments were
the most distinctive characteristics
between the two works. The two min
uets, the adagio cantabile for the first
violin, accompanied by other strings,
and . short dashing finale were pleas
ing and apply expressed the title.


Technical facility Of fingers and
bowing serve the artists well whenever
speed Is required, and no matter how
fast the tempo, each note stands out
clear and distinct Many times, how
ever, their tempt give the impression

within their capability. Accuracy OF
intonation and rhythmical precision
formed the background Of the presen-
tation yesterday and the players glided
effortlessly through the most compn-
Gated passages. Yet one felt that this
very facility stands somewhat Is .
drawback to q finer achievement In
nuance and tone color.


The program concluded with Mali
piero's Quartet No. t." modern work
written in one movement. Although
the idiom is strictly original and mod
ern, II has moments when one y con.
scious Of the nationality Of the COM
poser because Of the warmth that per-
neates the work. Good craftsman-
ship, vigor and occasional flights OF
lyricism, relieving the dissonance OF
the whole, contain that quality which
holds the interest Of the listener and
the discriminating group which visits
these concerts found 1t most enjoyable.

Two women and three men, all

SULLIVAN, Ind, Juy 16.-State
and Federal investigators CROPPED to-
day through fog Of gloom envelop-
Ing this community for an explana-
ton of a sudden underground gas ex-
plosion which cost the lives Of 20
coal miners.


Scared, mangled bodies Of the VIC
tins, removed from the scene OF the
blast 2l2 feet below the surface Of
the Glendora Coal Co.'S Baker mine
near here, were taken to Sullivan's
two mortuaries, where reatives sadly
claimed them.


Families Of the dead miners were
still too grieved to talk about funeral
plans. Friends said, however. tenta-
tive arrangements would call for sep
Arate services and burials.


Nine other miners were injured,
four seriously enough to remain in
Mary Sherman Hospital here. Two
Of them may die.


ia Miners Escape.


One hundred seventy-four miners
escaped the force OF the explosion
yesterday. They organized rescue ef-
forts and brought the injured to the
surface, but fire and poisonous gases
prevented them from reaching the
dead.


Many Of the survivors were sum-
moned to a formal inquest ordered
by Coroner Cecil B. Taylor for this
morning.


Representatives of the Federal
Bureau Of Mines, the State Bureau
Of Mines and Mining and the Indiana
Coal Operators Association joined in
an investigation of the disaster, one
Of the worst in Indiana's mining his
tory.


c. w. Templeton, part owner Of
the mine, expressed belief there were
two explosions, smaller one before
the final death-dealing blast He
said he believed they were caused by
gas pockets set off by miners open
carbide lamp.


Criticizes Workers Stand.


Templeton criticized the United
Mine Workers Organization for op-
posing the use OF electric lamps, de-
claring. had these lamps been used.
this tragedy would not have occurred"


Miners oppose electric bug lights"
because, they say. the lamps are too
heavy and acid from the batteries
damages their clothing.


Other mine officials said a spark
from the electric trolley of the mine
train might have ignited the gas.


Carbon monozide fumes which filled
the mine after the explosions pre-
vented removal of the victims bodies
for several hours. Then accompanied
by shrill blasts from the mine whistle,
the bodies were slowly brought to
the surface while more than 1000
anxious friends, relatives and volun-
teers stood near the mine opening.

Contour of the throat, which Is

The main supporting muscles Of

ened by the following exercises:

Position: Feet together, trunk

Movement: Continue bending

back down toward floor but keep
ing the abdominal muscles tense.

should feel a strong stretch in all

LOS ANGELES, Nov. 27-A million
tons of earth and rock tumbled down
Elysian Parks moving mountain"
last night, and today engineers fore
cast another even greater avalanche.


Three workmen narrowly escaped
when the landslide, 400 feet long,
spilled into scenic Riverside Drive,

Extra police barred sightseers from

Representatives of the city engineers

said the slide probably was only the
forerunner of a greater avalanche,
which might tumble from the summit,
destroying the Dayton Avenue Bridge
and clogging the Los Angeles River
bed.


Last nights slide came from the
mid-section of Buena Vista Peak.


Mile From Downtown Area.

the downtown business area. The
moving mountain is about $50 feet
in height.


Boulders, earth and trees spread last
night across Riverside Drive for ap-
proximately 400 feet, overflowing into
the Los Angeles River bed. The debris
piled up to a depth Of more than 40
feet in places.


The debris wrecked portions Of the
Riverside Drive viaduct.
About 100 feet of the drive was car
ried away in the slide.
The mountain has been under con-
stant watch by geologists and engi-
neers since the earth movement first

NEW YORK, october 16.-Com-
modify prices rallied moderately this
week, with upturns in farm staples
more than offsetting continued weak
ness in industrial items.


Foods. live stock and agricultural
products were included among gain
ers; textiles. non-ferrous metals and
other industrial commodities declined.
Quotations hit a new low for the
year on Monday, but, despite crum-
bling stock prices, recovered.


The Associated Press weighted index
Of IS important wholesale staple spot
prices rose to $500 per cent of the
1925 average, from 1921 a week ago
and compared with 8l.29 last year.

Cotton was bid up briskly. Some
quarters said the upturn was in part
a rebound from the drastic slump Of
last week. Demand for finished goods
also picked up. pushing consumption
above production for the first time
since last July. Then, too. the huge
crop was believed to have brought
output control nearer.

rising fractions, corn and rye slip
ping.

ward path this week. Cattle and lambs

tering the market basket nudged

LITTLE ROCK, Ark, January 23.-
Crumbling levees and slowly rising
flood waters drove thousands Of per-
sons from the lowlands Of Northeast
Arkansas today while freezing weather
left the State locked in an ice sheath
which an official estimated had done
100000 damage to timber lands.


At least two persons were known
dead in the flood area. but CRIPPLED
communication lines and inundated
highways prevented any accurate
check.


H. D. Booth. State highway traffic
supervisor, reported so roads under
water.


Red Cross Mobilizes.


The American Red Cross, mobiliZing
for action, sent Disaster Relief Di-
rector Albert Evans here.


Gov. Carl E. Bailey ordered the
Arkansas National Guard to send 1900
tents and three trucks to Blythville,
near Memphis. concentration point
for Mississippi County refugees.


The subfreezing weather was cold
est Of the year. The Weather Bureau
forecast low of 18 degrees tonight.


State Forester Charles Gillett esti-
mated the ice storm did $4,000, 900
damage to the State's s22 1000, 900

Dyess Col0nists Flee.


Little Rocks Camp Pike became
the concentration point for $500 Dyess
colony refugees who evacuated their
model homes last night when Big Lake
levee broke.


The colonists. taken to Wilson in
box cars. reported severe suffering.
They proceeded to Memphis in reg
ular coaches, spent the remainder OF
the night there and came here today.


Carl Hunt, 33, Ettawah volunteer
levee guard, froze to death at Big
Lake. Deputy Sheriff Tip Sullivan
Of Parkin reported the drowning of an
unidentified woman at Manila.

BOWIE, Md, March 27.-Scores
Of race horses, here for the spring
race meet which starts next week,
were endangered when fire broke
out at the track late last night.


Whipped by a strong wind, the
flames damaged an unoccupied
stable, then swept into the adjoin-
ing woods and burned over sew
eral acres before the volunteer
fire departments Of Bowie and
Glen Burnie and a number Of CCC
camp workers brought the blaze
under control.


More than 400 horses, including
Accolade, valued at more than
$4,000, are stabbed at the track
for the opening next Thursday.


Although the stable damaged
last night was empty at the time,
some "a horses had been assigned
to it and would have arrived in
the next few days. Damage from
the blaze was estimated at around
$4,000.

Anacostia Senior-Junior High
School will have its own green
house with the opening of the new
south wing some day this week,
Jere Crane, assistant superinteno-
ent in charge of business affairs
of the District public schools, said
today. The north wing is still in
the process of construction.


The school, which has been
operating as a junior high pending
completion of the new wing, will
not only graduate it's own students
into the senior high, but will take
about $50 more AnacoStia residents
from Eastern. Altogether, John
Paul Collins, principal, figures that
about 500 students will enter the
senior department for the first
time this February.


Beside the greenhouse the new
wing contains two biology rooms,
one physics and one chemistry
laboratory, one classroom, music
room and gymnasium with fold
ing partition for both junior and
senior students.


1t also provides for physical di
rectors' rooms, showers and lock-
ers. In the basement will be an
armory for military activities.
The school will have it's own cadet
corps this semester, Mr.. Crane,
who designed the wing, said.


In the rear of the present build
ing will be woodworking and metal
shops for both senior and Junior
students.

CENTERVILLE, Ind, Dec. 25.-
Sheriff Arthur Quigley Of Wayne
County said today he believed two
former convicts made the crude and
unsuccessful Christmas eve attempt
to extort $4,000 from John L. Bryan,
Centerville State Bank cashier, by
grabbing 3-year-old Donald Bryan, the
bankers only son.


Neither the sheriff nor Indiana and
Ohio State police had found any
trace however, of the men who es-
capped, leaving behind, unharmed, the
boy, his mother. nursemaid and a
grocery clerk, all of whom were car
ried away from the Bryan home.


The sheriff said he based his theory
that the men were convicts on de-
scriptions by the nurse. 17-year-old
Norma Schroy, and Julian Dunbar,
the grocery clerk, and statements that
the pair wore gloves, apparently as a
precaution against leaving finger
prints.


Automobile Still Missing.


Although wide search continued
throughout Christmas Day, officers
found neither the Bryan family au-
tomobile, in which one of the men
fled from the home, carrying with
him Mrs. Bryan and Dunbar, nor the
kidnaper's car, in which the other
man drove away with the boy and
the nursemaid.


Mrs. Bryan and Dunbar were re-
leased at New Lisbon, several miles
east Of Centerville, and the child and
the nursemaid were put off the other
machine at Greensboro, in Northern
Wayne County.


The two men entered the Bryan
home late yesterday, Miss Schroy told
officers. and at the point of revolvers
instructed her to summon home Mrs.
Bryan, who was with her husband
ut the bank.


The men told Mrs. Bryan upon her
arrival to telephone her husband to
bring home $1,000 at once. The tele-
phone call was answered, however, by
Mark Stevens, the bank president, and
Stevens. sensing something wrong, or
ganized a posse and with Bryan hur-
ried to the house.


Forced Into Cars.


The kidnapers, apparently impa-
tient and fearful, ordered Miss Schroy
to take her charge and get into their
car Mrs. Bryan and the grocery clerk
who had arrived to make a delivery,
and who had been forced by the men
to come into the house, were COM
PEELED to enter the Bryan car.


The two cars were driven away as
the posse led by Stevens approached
Stevens exchanged shots with the kid
naper in the Bryan car.


Sheriff Quigley said the men made
no threats against the Bryan boy, but
the kidnaper who took Dunbar and
Mrs. Bryan away threatened to kill
them


Bryan and his wife, shaken by their
experience, left Centerville today tell
ing friends they would be gone several
days. They were reported to have
gone to Darlington, Ind, to visit rela-
tives Of Mrs. Bryan.

strikes in the steel industry would dull

allowed prices to sink fractions to
around 2 points.

through served to cut the entire list
from price moorings, brokers said.

that declines were registered on lin

ment.

The Illinois State Society will hold
a Valentine dance tonight in the
little ball room at the Willard
Hotel from to o'clock.

those who do not wish to dance.

delegation, headed by Mrs. James
Hamilton Lewis and Mrs. William
Dieterich, will turn the gayety into
cheer for the Illinois flood sufferers.
Mrs. Lewis and Miss Clara Hope will
read the future and fortunes of con-
tributors to the flood relief fund. Mrs.
Dieterich and Mrs. Ruth Kalthoff,
with the wives of several Congressman,
are providing punch, candies and
flowers, the profits to be for flood

SANTA MONICA, Cal, Feb. 25.
Fighting broke out here today be-
tween company guards and sit
down strikers in the huge Douglas
Aircraft Company's plant.


The guards emerged victorious
after forcing the strikers out Of
the engineering department of the
plant after what they termed
some scuffling."


The trouble started when
handful of the 300 sit-downers
broke through the door into the
engineering department. where
men had worked yesterday in de-
fiance of the strike.


Twelve guards rushed in from
the outside and struggled with the
strikers, forcing them back into
the quarters they have occupied
for two days and two nights. No
arrests were made.


It was the first row between
officers and the strikers since the
big plant closed down, tieing up
$25,000,000 worth of orders and
throwing $500 men out of work.


Meanwhile the company was ex-
pected to go to court today after
the strikers decided to ignore
company order that they evacuate.
At the same time company off
cials were invited to a peace con-
ference" set by strike leaders for
late today.


Whether Donald D. Douglas,
young inventive genius who heads
the corporation, would accept the
invitation extended by DR.. Towne
Nylander, regional head of the Ma
tional Labor Relations Board,
was uncertain.


Meanwhile the American Fed
Grafton of Labor unions at the
plant appeared to have broken
definitely with the United Auto
mobile Workers Union, whose
aircraft division local is sponsor
ing the strike, claiming discrimi-
nation against its members.

LONDON.-This year marks the
tercentenary of the foundation of the
premier body of bell ringers in the
world. The Ancient Society of COL
lege Youths was formed in London
by noblemen and city aldermen in
1887. Bells have played their part
in English history, having been used
in early days to call or rouse the
burghers to arms.


In early times the Seeding Bell told
the farmer when to plant and the
Harvest Bell to make ready for thresh-
ing, and every week the Oven Bell.
when the church warders had pre-
pared the spacious communal facili-
tles OF the parish oven, sent each
housewife with her daughters and
small sons scurrying with pans of
dough. There also was the Cleaning
Bell which told the poor to begin
gathering corn in the fields and the
Mote Bell that summoned those ouali-
ned to attend court The Curfew Bell
still survives in many places. but the
Waking Bell has lately fallen into
disuse.

NEW YORK, September 18.-Com-
modify prices advanced for the second
consecutive period this week, follow
| ing an unbroken decline of two
months.


Industrial and agricultural staples
continued to follow divergent paths,
the former sinking steadily and the
latter advancing sharply.


The Associated Press weighted index
of 35 important wholesale commodi-
ties moved ahead to 1924 per cent
of the 1926 average from 86.74 week
ago and compared with 8l.47 last
year.


The upSwing was by no means
unanimous, however, the number of
staples chalking up better prices being
equaled by those showing losses. The
decisiveness of the gain was largely
the result of strength in heavily
weighted items. such as corn, live
stock and butter.


Live Stock Higher.


Live stock quotations swept up to
higher ground, bid up to the best
levels for the year by dealers who had
relatively small stocks on hand and
were faced with official estimates that
shipments to market would taper off
considerably the next few months.
Hogs, cattle and lambs shared the
squirt, with the latter showing the
best gain.


With corn rising sensationally on
continued reports of crop damage,
farm staples pushed ahead despite de-
clines in wheat, oats and cotton. Rye
advanced with the heavily weighted
corn.


Food was marked up, gains in eggs.
lard and butter overbalancing sinking
spells in sugar, cocoa, coffee and -four
Demand has been heavy for table
items, commodity men reported, and
the available supply limited in some
cases.


Textiles Hit New Low.


Although a minor rally developed
at the close Of the week, textiles slip
ped into new low ground for the year.
The same bearish influence, diversified
inventories, hung over the market.
Leaders in the industry, however, have
taken cognizance Of the situation and
efforts were made to reduce bloated
stocks. Pacific Mills, one of the
biggest manufacturers, cut operations
to three days week and other pro-
ducers were believed considering the
move


A sharp break in steel scrap prices
tumbled industrial commodities. Rub
ber, coal and burlap also fell back.
Turpentine, lumber, antimony and tin

ics; for the first five years he averaged

robi. Kenya Colony, Philip Whit
marsh, millionaire Canadian gold
miner and his wife were rescued by
the movie expedition headed by Mrs.
Osa johnson, the expedition radioed
its ofices here last night.


The Whitmarshes, the message said
were flying to Nairobi to meet the ex-
pedition when their plane crashed in
a forced landing. They were without
food for four days until q searching
party reached them.


The expedition Is making a picture
about the experiences of Livingstone
and Stanley, the lost" explorer and
the newspaper man who found him


1t is Mrs. Johnsons first trip since
her recovery from injuries received In
the West Coast airplane crash in
which her husband, Martin johnson
was killed.

Hearings in the complaint OF the
National Labor Relations Board that
the Willard Hotel discharged Mrs.
Mabel Norman, coffee shop waitress,
for testimony against the manage
ment in a previous case were in re-
cess today Upon resumption next
Monday, Harry Sommerville, hotel
manager, is scheduled to testify


Yesterday the board heard Miss
Evelyn Miller, manager of the shop,
and Miss Mary Brim, hostess, testify
that Mrs. Norman had become in
creasingly arrogant" after joining
the Hotel and Restaurant Workers
Alliance.


Miss Brim, stately blond, who
said she went to college in st. Louis
and managed a restaurant in Chi
cago before coming to the Willard,
said she thought the Willard shop
was beautifully operated" when she
came here, but that conditions start
ed getting bad when the mattresses
joined the union, and became "un-
bearable" after Mrs Norman ap-
peared in the previous hearing


Miss Brim also told Trial Exam
liner Edwin S. Smith that she would
not only have fired Mrs. Norman,
but would have fired the whole
bunch" when they made some pro-
test just before January l about
signing new contract cards. Such
conduct, she explained, was in
subordination," adding during cross
examination that to her mind any
protest to the management about any,
thing constituted INSTRUMENTATION I"


The hostess admitted hoping Mrs.
Norman would quit and admitted try
Ing to make it uncomfortable" for
her after the testimony under dispute.


She said she was afraid for the
safety of the non-union girls in the
kitchen, where union cooks were de-
laying their orders and where "hot
water might be spilled on them"

ONLY DIFFERENCE


The high tribunals decision was

accused Of controlling, either di-
rectly or indirectly, through a
maze Of interlocking directorates,
the major anthracite producing
companies and the principal hard
coal carrying railroads.

Just as when the court and Fed
eral Trade Commission first as
sailed it from 1915 to 1920. the
present connection between the
coal producers and coal carriers
mitigates against cheap anthra-
cite, the Pennsylvania commission

cooking gas Bolder citizens who
closed the doors and opened the burn

camp is fully equipped with shelter

with skis a week ago when lakes and
rivers showed strong ice surfaces.

ever, honeycombed and weakened the
ice in places. The plane carried
emergency rations for several days.

morning.

bed in their one-story cottage at

were Virginia. II, and Marie, S.

her husband, Turiaf Galley, and her
son Gustov went to work, then hit the
girls over the head "15 or 20 times"
and told neighbor what she had done.

man arrested the woman. The district
attorney said he was convinced she
was "a mental case" and that he
would have a committee of physicians
appointed to examine her. He stated ::


She didn't seem at all sorry about

wanted to kiss the bodies before We
took her away.


she said she hit the older girl in

British officials said today that
Prime Minister Joseph A. Lyons
victory in the Australian elections
last Saturday would accelerate
negotiations for an Anglo-Amer-
lean trade treaty.

Talks about new trade past
have been in progress since the
visit of Daniel C. Roper, United
States Secretary of Commerce, to
England in 1896, and have been
revived from time to time, but
without result.


The British have maintained
that no agreement could come
without the acquiescence Of the
British dominions. The Canadians
wish to see the conclusion of an
Anglo-American trade pact.


AWAITED ELECTIONS


The views of some other domin-
ions on the subject are also before
the authorities here. But, it has
been stated that Australia could
not come to any decision until
after the elections, because Prime
Minister Lyons hands were tied
until then.

BY the Associated Press.


HONG KONG. September III
Daring. death-defying aviators fought
today the first great aerial battle Of
the Sino-Japanese War over Canton,
South China city 100 miles to the
north of this British-owned city.


At least six, possibly 10, japanese
planes crashed in twisting, diving dog
fights. One Chinese pursuit plane
was seen to crash in flames. Others
also may have fallen.


A bomb demolished the Tingho
Aviation School Administration Build
ing. Other bombs narrowly missed
the Saichuen cement works. A num-
Der of civilians were reported killed.


Battle Started in Early Morning.


A feet of 81 Japanese raiding ships
started the battle, appearing at early
morning in an offensive directed
against the far South China city.


Ten planes make second attack
shortly after noon.


Residents along the Canton River
front had a thrilling view of the
combat.


Only half of the squadron of 81 ac-
tually reached Canton itself, Chinese
said. Others were brought down by
defending Chinese pursuit planes and
artillery fire from forts in the Canton
area.


One raider, diving and twisting to
ward of attackers, crashed to the
ground. His plane exploded and the
crew of two was killed.


Another japanese ship fell near
White Cloud Mountain. Three occu-
pants died. The one Chinese plane
which residents saw falling went down
in flames. The pilot. wounded and
burned, landed by parachute.


More Than 10 Bombs Dropped.


The japanese attackers dropped
more than 10 bombs in the morning
raid. directing their aim at Chinese
airdromes. The bombs fell, however
into surrounding fields. Several farm
ers were injured.


The Aviation School was bombed in
the second raid. One japanese ship
was forced down and its three occu-
pants were taken prisoner. Two other
planes, obviously badly damaged,
turned in fight.


Although many civilians were re-
ported killed, Canton buildings suffered
little damage. 1t is believed here that
the planes came from the aircraft
tender Notoro, said to be maneuvering
just outside the mouth of the Canton
River.
